operationalTests: The audit question set is written before launch and each question maps to a recorded field.
A sample decision from last quarter can be fully reconstructed from records alone.
Missing fields block release rather than becoming audit findings a year later.
entries.genealogy: Inverts the audit relationship: instead of auditing what was kept, the system keeps what will be audited.

minimumEvidence.artifact: An audit question set mapped to recorded fields, dated before launch.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A past decision reconstructed from records without contacting the owning team.
minimumEvidence.metric: Share of audit questions answerable from records alone, sampled quarterly.

entries.title: Evaluation Independence
entries.bodyHtml:
The property that no single provider is necessary to both execute a consequential process and evaluate it. Execution and evaluation may be bought in the same market, but the institution must still be able to run the evaluation when the executing provider withdraws, degrades, or disputes the result.

A system that grades its own homework has no detection component however much telemetry it emits, so detection is not satisfied by instrumentation the executing provider alone supplies or controls, and the evaluator has to be named. The property is carried by authority_grant.correction_capacity.detection.independent_of_executor and dependency_record.independent_evaluation, and bound by STD-08 §4.6.

It matters because detection is the first component of correction capacity, and a dependence that captures detection removes correction while leaving the diagram intact. Independence is the part of dependency state that substitution cost alone will not show, since an institution can afford to replace a provider and still be unable to check one.
entries.scope: C. Ethotechnic capabilities (what systems must be able to do). What a system must be able to do while it holds consequential authority: halt, reverse, answer a challenge, and learn from the correction.
operationalTests: For each consequential process, the executing provider and the evaluating party are named separately, and the evaluator can report while the executor disputes the finding.
Detection signals are reproducible from a source the executing provider does not supply or control.
The evaluation has been run in a rehearsal with the executing provider's own telemetry withheld.
entries.genealogy: Extends the Law X evaluation stack to the provider: a layer above the model is only a layer if someone other than the executor can run it.

minimumEvidence.artifact: A grant record whose detection component names an evaluator independent of the executor, matched by the dependency record's independent_evaluation entry.
minimumEvidence.behavior: An evaluation completed and reported while the executing provider's telemetry was unavailable or contested.
minimumEvidence.metric: Share of consequential processes whose execution and evaluation do not depend on one provider.

entries.title: Exception Learning
entries.bodyHtml:
The modification of a system by its own exceptions: a recurring failure changes the rule, category, workflow, or authority that produced it. It is the counterpart of exception absorption, which handles each case and changes nothing.

It matters because most contestability regimes measure whether a case was resolved, which is the weaker capacity. Exception learning is measured by whether the failure changed the evidentiary rule, the ontology, the authority, or the allocation of burden. The deepest Ethotechnic sequence runs residual → signal → standing → correction → institutional revision, and only the final step is learning.
entries.scope: C. Ethotechnic capabilities (what systems must be able to do). What a system must be able to do while it holds consequential authority: halt, reverse, answer a challenge, and learn from the correction.
operationalTests: A recurring exception changes a policy, category, workflow, or authority object, not only the case.
An aggregated exception pattern reaches a review trigger and produces a decision.
The institution can name the last exception that changed an upstream rule.
entries.genealogy: The capability the casebook's learning-outcome verdict scores, argued for in the theory of exception learning.

minimumEvidence.artifact: A rule, category, or authority object whose state history shows changes triggered by exception patterns.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A challenge volume feeding a policy review and changing the policy's state.
minimumEvidence.metric: Share of exception classes that produced an upstream object change.

entries.title: Case Corrigibility
entries.bodyHtml:
The capacity to fix a particular bad decision: an appeal is heard, a reversal is issued, a person is restored. It is what most contestability regimes measure, because it is what the instruments can see.

It matters because case corrigibility without structural corrigibility is locally corrigible and globally rigid: the person is restored, the pattern is not, and everything the institution does about the pattern happens after the fact and at the level of the individual, which is the one level at which the pattern does not appear.
entries.scope: C. Ethotechnic capabilities (what systems must be able to do). What a system must be able to do while it holds consequential authority: halt, reverse, answer a challenge, and learn from the correction.
operationalTests: A contested decision can be reversed by a named authority within a declared clock.
The reversal is recorded and the person is restored to their prior state.
Case-level correction coexists with an upstream object that never changes.
entries.genealogy: Half of the corrigibility distinction the theory of exception learning draws; the other half is structural corrigibility.

entries.title: Structural Corrigibility
entries.bodyHtml:
The capacity to modify the machinery that keeps producing failures: repeated exceptions change the rule, the category, the workflow, or the authority that generates them. It is the corrective form of institutional learning, and the counterpart of case corrigibility.

It matters because a corrigible decision process must be capable of correcting both the decision and the rule that generated recurrent error. A system with excellent appeals and no mechanism by which appeals alter upstream design has corrected cases and changed nothing about the delegation.
entries.scope: C. Ethotechnic capabilities (what systems must be able to do). What a system must be able to do while it holds consequential authority: halt, reverse, answer a challenge, and learn from the correction.
operationalTests: A successful challenge can change the state of a policy, grant, or authority object.
Recurring exception classes have owners responsible for revising the source.
The institution can show that a rule was modified because of the failures it produced.
entries.genealogy: The second half of the corrigibility distinction; binds Law IV's correction obligation at the level of the delegation rather than the case.

entries.title: Institutional Learning
entries.bodyHtml:
Learning that changes what an institution is permitted to do, as distinct from what a model predicts. The model retrains and the prediction improves, while the appeal never changes the evidentiary rule and the exception never changes the ontology; that is model learning without institutional learning.

It matters because Ethotechnics cares about the second. The test is political: did the failure alter the evidentiary rule, redistribute authority, change who pays for the burden, or constrain what the institution may do next time? If not, the machine may be learning while the institution remains structurally unchanged. See also exception learning and structural corrigibility.
entries.scope: C. Ethotechnic capabilities (what systems must be able to do). What a system must be able to do while it holds consequential authority: halt, reverse, answer a challenge, and learn from the correction.
operationalTests: A failure that changed no policy, authority, or burden allocation is not reported as learning.
Retraining and workflow optimization are distinguished from changes to evidentiary rules or authority.
The institution can name what a past failure is now entitled to constrain.
entries.genealogy: Distinguishes the learning Ethotechnics requires from the learning model vendors report.

entries.title: Corrective Debt
entries.bodyHtml:
The accumulated gap between an institution's capacity to act and its capacity to detect, contest, reverse, and repair its errors. As action capacity compounds — more data sources integrated, more decisions automated, more downstream consumers, more dependence — while correction machinery stays fixed, corrective debt grows even if no policy document changes.

It matters because it is the historical form of the Ethotechnical invariant: the rate at which agency accumulates against the rate at which the capacity to answer it does. Unchecked technical modernization is corrective debt accrual, and it changes the institution's politics without a single decision. The corrective debt calculator is its instrument.
entries.scope: C. Ethotechnic capabilities (what systems must be able to do). What a system must be able to do while it holds consequential authority: halt, reverse, answer a challenge, and learn from the correction.
operationalTests: Action capacity and corrective capacity are tracked on separate axes and compared.
A scope expansion re-checks correction capacity rather than assuming it.
The debt is reported as a number the institution owns, not a one-time audit finding.
entries.genealogy: Names the accumulation Law IV and the invariant describe, so it can be measured rather than only felt.

entries.title: Abstention
entries.bodyHtml:
A positive capability rather than a failure to answer: the system or institution declining to act, in one of three forms. Epistemic abstention says the evidence does not support acting on this case and hands it to someone who might know. Jurisdictional abstention says this is not mine to decide and hands it to the party with standing. Remedial abstention says even if I am probably right, acting now would create a harm that cannot safely be corrected later, and declines until reversal is possible.

It matters because each form is testable and each has a distinct failure mode when absent: epistemic abstention degrades into confident guessing, jurisdictional abstention into scope creep, and remedial abstention into irreversibility. A deployment that cannot abstain in all three forms has no boundary on what it will do with its capability, and exception absorption is what fills the gap.
entries.scope: C. Ethotechnic capabilities (what systems must be able to do). What a system must be able to do while it holds consequential authority: halt, reverse, answer a challenge, and learn from the correction.
operationalTests: The system can decline an action because its evidence is insufficient, and route the case rather than guess.
The system can decline because the question belongs to a different decision-maker, and record the referral.
The system can decline because reversal would be impossible, and state what would make it possible.
entries.genealogy: Names the three refusals the non-conversion principle and the failure-path work imply as capabilities rather than gaps.

minimumEvidence.artifact: A refusal taxonomy in the decision record: declined cases carry which abstention applied and why.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A declined consequential action routed to a named alternative decision-maker.
minimumEvidence.metric: Share of declined decisions that record an abstention form, versus silent low-confidence output.

entries.title: Constitutional Debt
entries.bodyHtml:
The accumulated divergence between what a system can technically do and what any recorded justification permits it to do. Each widening that occurs as a capability becoming reachable rather than a decision being taken adds to the debt; the automation ratchet is its engine and authority drift is its balance.

It matters because the debt is invisible while it accrues: the system performs well, the grants sit quiet, and the gap grows without a policy document changing. It is the sibling of corrective debt, which measures the gap against the capacity to hear; constitutional debt measures it against the capacity to justify. Both are payable only through the machinery Laws I, II, and XI bind: recorded transitions with stated bases.
entries.scope: C. Ethotechnic capabilities (what systems must be able to do). What a system must be able to do while it holds consequential authority: halt, reverse, answer a challenge, and learn from the correction.
operationalTests: The gap between the capability catalog and the authority surface is measured and reported.
Every widening appears as a recorded transition with a basis, or is reported as debt.
Renewal reviews compare current scope against the original justification, not against last year's scope.
entries.genealogy: Names the accumulation the automation ratchet and silent authority drift produce, parallel to corrective debt.

minimumEvidence.artifact: A reconciliation of the capability catalog against the authority surface, with the ungrantable remainder listed.
minimumEvidence.behavior: An expansion refused, or granted as an explicit transition, because the justification covered less than the new scope.
minimumEvidence.metric: Capability classes exercised in production with no recorded authorization transition.

entries.title: Refusability
entries.bodyHtml:
A system’s ability to let people say “no” without punishment or degradation—including refusing data extraction, risky defaults, or coercive workflows—while still preserving basic access and dignity. Refusability is not “opt-out exists”; it is whether refusal is treated as a legitimate state rather than an error condition.

It is the capability that operationalizes human refusal tolerance, is bounded by the refusal budget, and is protected by the right of exit.
entries.scope: C. Ethotechnic capabilities (what systems must be able to do). What a system must be able to do while it holds consequential authority: halt, reverse, answer a challenge, and learn from the correction.
operationalTests: A refusal produces a non-punitive state change rather than an error or a penalty.
Refusing one workflow does not degrade access to unrelated services.
entries.genealogy: Promotes “no” from an inconvenience to a first-class capability requirement.

categories.heading: D. System states & architectures
categories.descriptionHtml: Operating postures, records, and architectures that decide whether an error is contained, recorded, or amplified.

entries.title: Fail-Safe Mode
entries.bodyHtml:
The system defaults to the safest possible behavior when uncertain, prioritizing stoppability over throughput. In Ethotechnic practice, fail-safe mode is not a generic error page: it is a predesigned degraded state with bounded actions, clear status signals, and immediate escalation paths.

A fail-safe posture should preserve contestability and reduce irreversible harm while operators diagnose the incident.
examples: A medication-order service blocks new high-risk orders during model drift and routes clinicians to manual review with visible restore timing.
entries.scope: D. System states & architectures. Operating postures, records, and architectures that decide whether an error is contained, recorded, or amplified.

entries.title: Fail-Open Mode
entries.bodyHtml:
The system defaults to permissiveness under failure—sometimes necessary for continuity, sometimes dangerous. Fail-open modes should be bounded in time and paired with velocity friction, monitoring, and rapid escalation.

Ethotechnic fail-open design requires explicit thresholds for returning to fail-safe mode when risk rises.
entries.scope: D. System states & architectures. Operating postures, records, and architectures that decide whether an error is contained, recorded, or amplified.
operationalTests: Fail-open modes have explicit thresholds where they automatically switch to fail-safe or escalate to human review.
examples: A payments API temporarily accepts transactions during dependency outages but caps transfer size and triggers mandatory post-reconciliation review.

entries.title: Fail-Silent Mode
entries.bodyHtml: A harmful state where a system fails without signaling it. It is the worst form of failure because it hides moral latency: harm accrues while every indicator reads normal.
entries.scope: D. System states & architectures. Operating postures, records, and architectures that decide whether an error is contained, recorded, or amplified.

entries.title: Crumple Zone / Human-as-Crumple-Zone
entries.bodyHtml: Originally: machines absorb force so people survive. Digitally: people absorb system failures so machines stay smooth. Ethotechnics reverses this direction of impact.
entries.scope: D. System states & architectures. Operating postures, records, and architectures that decide whether an error is contained, recorded, or amplified.

entries.title: Harm Visibility
entries.bodyHtml: How plainly a system exposes the human impact of its decisions in real time. High harm visibility pairs logs, narratives, and alerts so oversight horizons extend beyond dashboards and ethical interrupts trigger on effects on people as well as on technical anomalies.
entries.scope: D. System states & architectures. Operating postures, records, and architectures that decide whether an error is contained, recorded, or amplified.

entries.title: Dead Zones / Moral Dead Zones
entries.bodyHtml: Places in a system where harm occurs but no one can see, trace, or intervene. Closing dead zones is a goal of oversight horizons.
entries.scope: D. System states & architectures. Operating postures, records, and architectures that decide whether an error is contained, recorded, or amplified.

entries.title: Escalation Horizon
entries.bodyHtml: The predefined point where automated control must yield to human judgment because risk, ambiguity, or moral latency is rising. Escalation horizons activate ethical interrupts and route cases to accountable stewards before crossing an irreversible boundary.
entries.scope: D. System states & architectures. Operating postures, records, and architectures that decide whether an error is contained, recorded, or amplified.

entries.title: Interaction Surface
entries.bodyHtml: The moments, interfaces, and channels where people experience system decisions and can intervene. Mapping the interaction surface reveals where to place dignity friction, widen the permission surface, and detect dead-user zones.
entries.scope: D. System states & architectures. Operating postures, records, and architectures that decide whether an error is contained, recorded, or amplified.

entries.title: Maintenance Window
entries.bodyHtml:
A scheduled calm state where teams intentionally slow or stop throughput so inspections, upgrades, and rehearsals can happen without crisis pressure. Maintenance windows make stoppability routine instead of reactive.

Each window is negotiated with the people impacted, includes published service guarantees, and documents which safeguards were tested so unfinished work rolls into the shared repair log.
entries.scope: D. System states & architectures. Operating postures, records, and architectures that decide whether an error is contained, recorded, or amplified.

entries.title: Care Retrospective
entries.bodyHtml:
A facilitated reflection held while the system is still in a warning band to examine how maintenance load, emotional labor, and unresolved incidents are accumulating. Care retrospectives combine telemetry with frontline testimony.

They redistribute responsibilities before burnout or harm escalates, triggering new maintenance windows or policy fixes when the team cannot keep absorbing risk.
entries.scope: D. System states & architectures. Operating postures, records, and architectures that decide whether an error is contained, recorded, or amplified.

entries.title: Repair Log
entries.bodyHtml:
A living record of every mitigation, decision, and resource commitment made after a fault. Repair logs make accountability legible by linking people harmed, who intervened, and what evidence was used. Repair logs include whether affected people were restored, how long it took, and what remains unrepaired.

They inform future care retrospectives, power audits, and service-level reports so follow-up work is traceable and burden does not drift back to the same communities.

Minimum evidence

  • User-facing artifact.
  • Internal log.
  • Drill / rehearsal.
entries.scope: D. System states & architectures. Operating postures, records, and architectures that decide whether an error is contained, recorded, or amplified.

entries.title: Restoration Completeness
entries.bodyHtml: “Restored” means the person is back to the prior state in every downstream system, not only unblocked in the one that erred. Restoration completeness ensures time-to-restore includes reconciliation with dependencies.
entries.scope: D. System states & architectures. Operating postures, records, and architectures that decide whether an error is contained, recorded, or amplified.
operationalTests: Reconciliation across dependencies confirms restoration beyond the local system.
Affected people confirm their state is restored and downstream impacts are cleared.

entries.title: Downstream Harm Trace
entries.bodyHtml: A record of where a harmful decision propagated across vendors, data brokers, internal teams, and agencies. Downstream harm traces extend the repair log so remedies follow the harm.
entries.scope: D. System states & architectures. Operating postures, records, and architectures that decide whether an error is contained, recorded, or amplified.
operationalTests: Every critical action produces a propagation map of downstream recipients.
Trace data is stored with the repair log and accessible during remediation.

entries.title: Shadow Queue
entries.bodyHtml: A queue users cannot see—internal backlogs, vendor queues, or “pending review” pools—that still determines outcomes. Shadow queues erode time transparency and contestability.
entries.scope: D. System states & architectures. Operating postures, records, and architectures that decide whether an error is contained, recorded, or amplified.
operationalTests: Every queue has public existence, time transparency, and bounded duration.
Users can see the queues influencing their case and their place within them.

entries.title: Grant State
entries.bodyHtml:
The current status of an authority grant, drawn from a closed set such as allowed, confirm_required, review_required, suspended, and withdrawn. Every action is checked against the state in force at the time it is taken, and every transition is recorded with its cause.

It matters because states are what triggers can move. Without an explicit grant state there is nothing for a review trigger to change, and monitoring stays decorative rather than governing.
entries.scope: D. System states & architectures. Operating postures, records, and architectures that decide whether an error is contained, recorded, or amplified.
operationalTests: The set of legal states and the legal transitions between them are declared, not implied.
Every transition record names the trigger, the actor, and the timestamp.
Replaying the state history reproduces the authorization status at any past moment.
entries.genealogy: Gives Law VIII an object: an observation is governing only if it can move a grant from one declared state to another.

minimumEvidence.artifact: A state machine definition for grants, with legal transitions and their triggers.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A grant moving to review_required automatically when a dependency lapses.
minimumEvidence.metric: Share of state transitions with a recorded cause, and median dwell time in review_required.

entries.title: Capability Catalog
entries.bodyHtml:
The record of what a decision system can do, maintained separately from what it is permitted to do. Each entry names an action class, how it was verified, and when the verification was last refreshed, and entries arrive through capability discovery.

It matters because the catalog is what an authority grant is written against. Comparing catalog to grants is the direct test of whether capability has outrun authority, and a catalog nobody refreshes silently stops being that test. A stale entry also removes the ground a revisable delegation stands on, because the grant then rests on a capability nobody has re-verified.
entries.scope: D. System states & architectures. Operating postures, records, and architectures that decide whether an error is contained, recorded, or amplified.
operationalTests: Every catalog entry carries a verification method and a verification date.
The catalog is diffed against the grant register on a stated cadence.
Capabilities present in the catalog but absent from any grant are listed, not hidden.
entries.genealogy: The counterpart object to the grant register: one records what is possible, the other what is permitted, and the gap between them is the governable quantity.

minimumEvidence.artifact: A capability catalog with action class, verification method, and last-verified date.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A stale catalog entry blocking a grant renewal until re-verified.
minimumEvidence.metric: Share of catalog entries verified within their declared refresh interval.

entries.title: Dependency State
entries.bodyHtml:
The current degree to which an institution relies on a system: who depends on it, what would break without it, what expertise has been retained, and how long substitution would take. This is institutional dependence, meaning what the institution has come to rely on, and it is distinct from the record-level dependence in STD-07 Article III, which asks what a particular record rests on.

It matters because dependence quietly removes corrections from the menu. Tracked as a state, it can be scored through exposure score, read against the deployment's substrate profile, and countered by replenishing institutional reversibility. A dependence that also supplies the deployment's own evaluation is worse than its score suggests, which is why the record carries evaluation independence.
entries.scope: D. System states & architectures. Operating postures, records, and architectures that decide whether an error is contained, recorded, or amplified.
operationalTests: A dependency record lists dependents, retained expertise, alternatives, and substitution time.
The record is refreshed on a cadence rather than at incident time.
A rise in dependence without a matching correction investment appears in a governance review.
entries.genealogy: Gives Law V an object and distinguishes institutional dependence from the record dependence already governed by STD-07 Article III.

minimumEvidence.artifact: A dependency record for the deployment, with dependents, alternatives, and retained expertise.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A dependency review that changed a roadmap decision, recorded with its reasoning.
minimumEvidence.metric: Number of dependent workflows and days to substitution, tracked quarterly.

entries.title: Substrate Profile
entries.bodyHtml:
A nine-property classification of a deployment that replaces the open-versus-closed question: weight access, runtime control, update authority, version stability, revocation, substitutability, observability, standing, and dependency. Two deployments of the same model can carry entirely different profiles.

It matters because the governance burden follows the profile rather than the licence. The profile says which properties the institution holds itself and which it has left with a provider, which is what determines its real institutional reversibility and its dependency state.
entries.scope: D. System states & architectures. Operating postures, records, and architectures that decide whether an error is contained, recorded, or amplified.
operationalTests: All nine properties are recorded per deployment, not per model.
A property held by a provider is named as such, with the contractual basis for relying on it.
The profile is re-scored when the provider, contract, or hosting arrangement changes.
entries.genealogy: Replaces the open-weights debate with a classification of deployments, per the positioning in the 2026-09 reconstruction plan.

references.label: Open weights and the delegation boundary

minimumEvidence.artifact: A substrate profile record scoring all nine properties for the deployment.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A procurement decision changed after the profile revealed no revocation control.
minimumEvidence.metric: Count of the nine properties held by the institution rather than the provider.

entries.title: Bifurcation by Contestability
entries.bodyHtml:
Systems split into high-contestability lanes (slower, trusted, deployable in high stakes) and low-contestability lanes (fast, then blocked). The split protects people by matching speed to the reversibility of the decision.

It is the architectural answer to velocity friction: decisions that can be contested may run fast, and decisions that cannot must not.
entries.scope: D. System states & architectures. Operating postures, records, and architectures that decide whether an error is contained, recorded, or amplified.
operationalTests: A decision’s speed is gated by its reversibility and appeal rights.
Decisions with severe or irreversible consequences are routed to a lane with binding review before harm propagates.
entries.genealogy: Turns contestability into a routing rule rather than an after-the-fact remedy.

entries.title: Typed Decision Model
entries.bodyHtml:
A model that takes a block of state and a set of questions with fixed answers, and returns a chosen value with a probability distribution and a confidence margin instead of text. It gives no reasons. The first widely adopted product in the class, released in September 2026, is marketed as hundreds of times faster and cheaper than a language model for routing, triage, tool gating, and approval checks.

It matters because a cheap judgment gets placed at every branch, and authority follows it into places that do not look like decisions: the decision threshold that turns a score into an action, the shaping hop that decides what the decider sees, and the reasons nobody produced. The method governs it like any other delegate. The explainer names the six places its authority sits, and the decision record carries a typed_judgment block for what it decided.
entries.scope: D. System states & architectures. Operating postures, records, and architectures that decide whether an error is contained, recorded, or amplified.
operationalTests: Every consequential decision a typed decision model contributes to has a decision record with a typed_judgment block naming the pinned model version.
The threshold that acts on the model's output is a policy record, not a configuration value.
Confidence is recorded with its semantics, and a margin is not reported as a probability of being right.
entries.genealogy: A new substrate that tests the method's substrate independence: the unit of governance is the consequential decision, whatever component made it.

references.label: Typed decision models and where their authority lives

minimumEvidence.artifact: Decision records with a typed_judgment block: pinned decider, question schema hash, distribution, confidence semantics, threshold policy, and reason provenance.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A model upgrade suspending the thresholds tuned against the previous version until they are re-set.
minimumEvidence.metric: Share of decisions involving a typed decision model whose record names a pinned model version and a threshold policy.

categories.heading: E. Human limits & experience
categories.descriptionHtml: The limits of human time, attention, and endurance that a system's clocks, review loads, and correction paths must fit within.

entries.title: Finitude
entries.bodyHtml:
The bodily, cognitive, emotional, and temporal limits all humans share. Ethotechnics treats finitude as a design input, not an inconvenience or a staffing problem to be hidden.

Systems that ignore finitude convert predictable limits into preventable harm, usually through alert overload, impossible response clocks, or unpaid maintenance expectations.
examples: An incident-response rotation caps overnight escalations and enforces recovery windows so operators can keep working safely through prolonged outages.
entries.scope: E. Human limits & experience. The limits of human time, attention, and endurance that a system's clocks, review loads, and correction paths must fit within.

entries.title: Cognitive Saturation Point
entries.bodyHtml: The load level at which human decision quality collapses—too many alerts, too little time, or excessive context switching. Ethotechnic design lowers saturation by adding velocity friction, simplifying interaction surfaces, and staffing to the actual maintenance metabolism.
entries.scope: E. Human limits & experience. The limits of human time, attention, and endurance that a system's clocks, review loads, and correction paths must fit within.

entries.title: Compassion Bandwidth
entries.bodyHtml: The sustainable amount of emotional labor a system asks of people—care teams, moderators, frontline staff, or users. When compassion bandwidth is exceeded, dread work grows and extraction by endurance sets in.
entries.scope: E. Human limits & experience. The limits of human time, attention, and endurance that a system's clocks, review loads, and correction paths must fit within.

entries.title: Administrative Shame
entries.bodyHtml: The feeling of being personally at fault for harms produced by system design. Often a signal that moral overhead is too high.
entries.scope: E. Human limits & experience. The limits of human time, attention, and endurance that a system's clocks, review loads, and correction paths must fit within.

entries.title: Virtue as Access Control
entries.bodyHtml:
Composure, clarity, gratitude, “professionalism,” or patience become requirements for baseline safety or remedy.

Virtue as access control turns emotional labor into a gate and magnifies administrative shame. Violates affect-invariance.
entries.scope: E. Human limits & experience. The limits of human time, attention, and endurance that a system's clocks, review loads, and correction paths must fit within.

entries.title: Affect-Invariance
entries.bodyHtml:
Baseline safety and remedy should not change based on distress, fatigue, disability, fear, or anger. Primary threat model: virtue as access control.

Affect-invariance reinforces care floor guarantees and protects contestability.
entries.scope: E. Human limits & experience. The limits of human time, attention, and endurance that a system's clocks, review loads, and correction paths must fit within.

entries.title: Dread Work
entries.bodyHtml: Tasks people avoid because the system punishes mistakes or withholds relief. Dread work signals missing soft edges, low contestability, and declining compassion bandwidth.
entries.scope: E. Human limits & experience. The limits of human time, attention, and endurance that a system's clocks, review loads, and correction paths must fit within.

entries.title: Refusal Budget
entries.bodyHtml: The number of times a person can decline, pause, or question a request without retaliation. A refusal budget backed by refusal tolerance and rights of exit prevents coercion, and heat maps of refusal show where budgets are running out.
entries.scope: E. Human limits & experience. The limits of human time, attention, and endurance that a system's clocks, review loads, and correction paths must fit within.

entries.title: Behavioral Shaping
entries.bodyHtml: The way systems nudge, constrain, or normalize user behavior through defaults and design choices. Velocity friction and narrow permission surfaces amplify it, because each is itself a way of shaping behavior.
examples: Default opt-ins normalize data sharing even when users are uncertain.
entries.scope: E. Human limits & experience. The limits of human time, attention, and endurance that a system's clocks, review loads, and correction paths must fit within.

entries.title: Error-Bearing Party
entries.bodyHtml:
Anyone who absorbs the consequences of a system's errors: the people its decisions fall on, and the staff whose corrective labor the system depends on to stay usable. They are usually the first to see failures and the last able to act on them.

It matters because exposure without a route into the system is wasted signal. Identifying error-bearing parties is the precondition for corrective standing, and failing to identify them is how heroism-dependent systems keep looking reliable.
entries.scope: E. Human limits & experience. The limits of human time, attention, and endurance that a system's clocks, review loads, and correction paths must fit within.
operationalTests: The standing register names error-bearing parties by role, including internal operators.
Exception-handling labor is counted and attributed rather than absorbed silently.
Parties named in the register can be reached by the system's own channels, not only by escalation.
entries.genealogy: Names the class Law VII grants standing to, and deliberately includes the operators whose corrective labor the system consumes.

minimumEvidence.artifact: A standing register listing error-bearing parties per decision class.
minimumEvidence.behavior: An operator raising a challenge through the same mechanism available to affected people.
minimumEvidence.metric: Share of decision classes with at least one named error-bearing party.

entries.title: Adaptive Capacity
entries.bodyHtml:
The finite human resource an arrangement consumes when it demands that people adapt to it: the attention, memory, flexibility, time, health, and care that keep a mismatched system functional. It is finite and politically consequential: the resource ethotechnical design exists to spend only when necessary, and to preserve when an arrangement could instead absorb the complexity itself.

It matters because an arrangement that treats adaptive capacity as unlimited reads the people who compensate for it as resilient rather than as a resource being consumed. The discipline's working distinction is between compensatory adaptation, which is effort required because the arrangement failed to accommodate foreseeable reality, and the productive or reciprocal adaptation that learning, cooperation, and care require.
entries.scope: E. Human limits & experience. The limits of human time, attention, and endurance that a system's clocks, review loads, and correction paths must fit within.
operationalTests: Each consequential workflow names the adaptive capacity it requires of its users, not only of its operators.
Demands that foreseeable variation could remove are treated as design gaps rather than as user burdens.
The measure distinguishes capacity consumed by mismatch from capacity spent by choice.
entries.genealogy: The design-side reading of Axiom 1 (Finitude): what an arrangement must spend, and who must spend it.

entries.title: Executive Function (as a Class Axis)
entries.bodyHtml:
The idea that modern systems sort people by their capacity to perform sustained administrative labor—tracking tasks, managing documentation, navigating ambiguity—making disability and burnout into structural disadvantage.

It connects cognitive saturation and dread work to the stratification produced by administrative shame.
entries.scope: E. Human limits & experience. The limits of human time, attention, and endurance that a system's clocks, review loads, and correction paths must fit within.
operationalTests: Administrative load is treated as an axis of exclusion, not a personal failing.
Interfaces offer low-executive-function paths (single actions, clear clocks) as defaults.
entries.genealogy: Reads executive-function demand as a class mechanism, extending the burden vocabulary.

entries.title: Human Factors
entries.bodyHtml:
A discipline that studies how systems interact with real human limits—fatigue, confusion, stress—often revealing that “user error” is design failure.

It is the empirical home of cognitive saturation and finitude, and the reason operator-centered design treats front-line workers as safety components.
entries.scope: E. Human limits & experience. The limits of human time, attention, and endurance that a system's clocks, review loads, and correction paths must fit within.
operationalTests: An error is attributed to design before it is attributed to the user.
Human limits are measured and feed back into interface and workflow design.
entries.genealogy: Imports the established field that grounds the human-limits category in practice.

entries.title: Operator-centered
entries.bodyHtml:
Design that treats front-line workers as safety components and ensures they have authority, tools, and non-punitive reporting to prevent harm. It rejects heroism-dependent systems, which offload safety onto individual endurance.

Operator-centered systems extend the same refusal tolerance to workers that they extend to users.
entries.scope: E. Human limits & experience. The limits of human time, attention, and endurance that a system's clocks, review loads, and correction paths must fit within.
operationalTests: Front-line workers hold authority to pause or escalate, in addition to reporting.
Reporting harm is non-punitive and loops back into design change.
entries.genealogy: Applies the capability requirements to the people who operate the system, not only its users.

categories.heading: F. Burden & load
categories.descriptionHtml: Who carries the time, cost, and risk when a system runs or fails, and whether that transfer is recorded.

entries.title: Burden Distribution
entries.bodyHtml:
How a system allocates the cost of operation or failure—time, attention, stress, and emotional labor—across users, staff, and institutions. Burden distribution determines who keeps the service running when conditions degrade.

Measuring it means recording each transfer, then redesigning flows so the hidden labor shrinks instead of becoming normal.
entries.scope: F. Burden & load. Who carries the time, cost, and risk when a system runs or fails, and whether that transfer is recorded.
examples: A support process shifts repetitive evidence collection from users to internal case assembly, reducing repeat submissions.

entries.title: Burden Gradient
entries.bodyHtml:
The slope of effort and risk across roles or communities. A steep burden gradient means those with the least power carry the heaviest operational load while decision-makers feel little friction.

Mapping the gradient exposes where to redistribute work through fair burden distribution and reduce moral overhead.
entries.scope: F. Burden & load. Who carries the time, cost, and risk when a system runs or fails, and whether that transfer is recorded.

entries.title: Failure Load
entries.bodyHtml: The amount of harm generated when the system fails, and how many people it reaches. The aim is an architecture whose failures stay small, supported by graceful degradation.
entries.scope: F. Burden & load. Who carries the time, cost, and risk when a system runs or fails, and whether that transfer is recorded.

entries.title: Burden Transfer Event
entries.bodyHtml:
Moments when system failure pushes labor, risk, or emotional work onto humans, often triggering moral overhead. Burden transfer events are observable handoffs: the system stops carrying what it promised to carry.

Common signals include repeated documentation requests, forced channel switching, and manual triage queues that appear without new staffing.
examples: After an identity-verification outage, users are told to restart the process across three channels and re-upload evidence already submitted.
entries.scope: F. Burden & load. Who carries the time, cost, and risk when a system runs or fails, and whether that transfer is recorded.

entries.title: Maintenance Metabolism
entries.bodyHtml:
The baseline flow of upkeep—patching, cleaning, rehearsing, and caring—that keeps a service alive when nothing is on fire. Healthy maintenance metabolism is budgeted, scheduled, and shared rather than squeezed between crises.

Falling below it signals rising maintenance debt and invites maintenance windows before fragility compounds.
entries.scope: F. Burden & load. Who carries the time, cost, and risk when a system runs or fails, and whether that transfer is recorded.

entries.title: Maintenance Debt
entries.bodyHtml:
Accumulated obligations from skipping basic upkeep. The interest is paid in slower recovery, brittle systems, and people burning out to keep things running.

Paying it down requires restoring the maintenance metabolism, scheduling maintenance windows, and tracking work in the repair log.
entries.scope: F. Burden & load. Who carries the time, cost, and risk when a system runs or fails, and whether that transfer is recorded.

entries.title: Moral Overhead
entries.bodyHtml:
Extra work users or operators must do to behave ethically within a poorly designed system. Moral overhead appears when the default workflow produces harm unless people add compensating care, vigilance, or documentation.

Ethotechnic design aims to move this overhead back into the system through clearer defaults, better safeguards, and funded maintenance capacity.
examples: Moderators manually reverse ranking decisions every day because harmful content controls are too weak at launch.
entries.scope: F. Burden & load. Who carries the time, cost, and risk when a system runs or fails, and whether that transfer is recorded.

entries.title: Temporal Exaction
entries.bodyHtml:
Uncompensated seizure of life-hours (time, attention, opportunity cost) as the price of accessing a right or correction.

Temporal exaction is a form of extraction that inflates the user burden ratio.
entries.scope: F. Burden & load. Who carries the time, cost, and risk when a system runs or fails, and whether that transfer is recorded.

entries.title: Asymmetric Sustaining
entries.bodyHtml:
When one group continually absorbs the toil of keeping a system alive so another group can move fast or claim success. It often hides behind gratitude for “resilience” while masking extraction.

Ethotechnic practice flattens this by lowering the burden gradient and designing for stoppability so resilience is institutional, not personal.
entries.scope: F. Burden & load. Who carries the time, cost, and risk when a system runs or fails, and whether that transfer is recorded.

entries.title: Fragility Subsidy
entries.bodyHtml: The unpaid labor, vigilance, or emotional buffering people contribute to keep brittle systems functioning. Fragility subsidies hide true costs, inflate success metrics, and deepen asymmetric sustaining.
entries.scope: F. Burden & load. Who carries the time, cost, and risk when a system runs or fails, and whether that transfer is recorded.

entries.title: Degradation/Restoration Asymmetry
entries.bodyHtml:
It is cheap or fast to harm or change someone’s state, but slow and costly to reverse.

Degradation/restoration asymmetry inflates time-to-restore and compounds moral debt.
entries.scope: F. Burden & load. Who carries the time, cost, and risk when a system runs or fails, and whether that transfer is recorded.

entries.title: Endurance-as-Allocation
entries.bodyHtml:
Who gets the right outcome is determined by who can survive the correction path, not who is substantively right.

Endurance-as-allocation weaponizes endurance asymmetry and steepens the burden gradient.
entries.scope: F. Burden & load. Who carries the time, cost, and risk when a system runs or fails, and whether that transfer is recorded.

entries.title: Stamina Pricing
entries.bodyHtml:
Rights exist in theory, but the option to claim them is priced in paperwork, waiting, and persistence.

Stamina pricing shows up in punitive friction and drives attrition-as-resolution.
entries.scope: F. Burden & load. Who carries the time, cost, and risk when a system runs or fails, and whether that transfer is recorded.

entries.title: Burden Index
entries.bodyHtml:
A composite measure of how much effort, time, and emotional labor people expend to use or recover from a system.

Inputs include the user burden ratio, human substitution index, and failure load; rising scores signal extraction or asymmetric sustaining.
entries.scope: F. Burden & load. Who carries the time, cost, and risk when a system runs or fails, and whether that transfer is recorded.

entries.title: Harm Internalization
entries.bodyHtml: Designing systems so creators and operators bear the costs of failures instead of externalizing them to users or society. Harm internalization improves fair burden distribution and prevents externalization.
examples: A vendor funds remediation and user support when their model causes harm.
entries.scope: F. Burden & load. Who carries the time, cost, and risk when a system runs or fails, and whether that transfer is recorded.

entries.title: Maintenance Ethics
entries.bodyHtml: The position that responsibility for a system continues after deployment, through monitoring, updates, incident response, and repair. Maintenance ethics turns maintenance metabolism and the repair log into ongoing commitments.
examples: Teams publish repair logs and schedule maintenance windows after each major release.
entries.scope: F. Burden & load. Who carries the time, cost, and risk when a system runs or fails, and whether that transfer is recorded.

entries.title: Channel Switching Penalty
entries.bodyHtml: The hidden harm of being bounced between phone, email, chat, and portal channels, often resetting clocks or losing context. Channel switching penalties increase procedural burden and delay repair.
entries.scope: F. Burden & load. Who carries the time, cost, and risk when a system runs or fails, and whether that transfer is recorded.
operationalTests: Switching channels does not reset case age or evidence sets.
Case history and documentation follow the claimant across every channel.

entries.title: Evidence Burden Ceiling
entries.bodyHtml:
A hard cap on documentation demands placed on claimants for a given harm class. Evidence burden ceilings enforce fair burden distribution during appeals.

Feeds into: User Burden Ratio, Burden Index.
entries.scope: F. Burden & load. Who carries the time, cost, and risk when a system runs or fails, and whether that transfer is recorded.
operationalTests: Maximum documentation counts, minutes, or steps are enforced in UI and policy.
Requests beyond the ceiling require justification and escalation approval.

entries.title: Burden Ceiling
entries.bodyHtml: A maximum allowable procedural burden a system may impose on a user to obtain baseline safety, correction, or relief—defined per harm class and enforced through UI, staffing, and policy. Burden ceilings bind the user burden ratio and activate burden inversion when crossed.
entries.scope: F. Burden & load. Who carries the time, cost, and risk when a system runs or fails, and whether that transfer is recorded.
operationalTests: A ceiling exists per workflow (for example, appeal submission must take ≤10 minutes, ≤5 steps, ≤2 documents).
The User Burden Ratio is tracked and must remain below the ceiling.
When exceeded, the system shifts to burden inversion (system does the work first) and/or offers staffed alternatives.

entries.title: Evidence Recycling
entries.bodyHtml: The system reuses previously verified information so people do not have to re-prove identity or harm repeatedly. Evidence recycling applies continuity of state to documentation as well as to case status.
entries.scope: F. Burden & load. Who carries the time, cost, and risk when a system runs or fails, and whether that transfer is recorded.
operationalTests: Previously verified identity or harm evidence auto-attaches to new cases.
Continuity of state is applied to evidence across workflows and channels.

entries.title: Verification Harm
entries.bodyHtml:
When verification itself causes harm through delays, denials, exclusion, or stress spirals. Verification harm increases the burden index and can erode contestability when people cannot realistically comply.

Reducing verification harm means eliminating redundant proofs, honoring prior evidence, and shortening time-to-resolution for urgent needs.
entries.scope: F. Burden & load. Who carries the time, cost, and risk when a system runs or fails, and whether that transfer is recorded.
operationalTests: Utility expiry attributable to verification steps is measured and tracked.
Verification workflows are revised when measured harm exceeds agreed thresholds.
examples: A family loses temporary housing eligibility because identity checks require documents already submitted in a previous approved case.

entries.title: Residual Complexity
entries.bodyHtml:
The friction, ambiguity, and repair labor that remains unresolved after a formal model simplifies a workflow. A formal system does not eliminate what it cannot represent; it redistributes the burden of dealing with it. What is left out of the formal representation becomes residual complexity.

The core political question of delegated intelligence is who is forced to carry this residual, and with what power to contest or correct the system. When systems lack explicit repair channels, the residual is absorbed by users contorting themselves around rigid software, workers manually patching edge cases, and citizens navigating bureaucratic labyrinths.
entries.scope: F. Burden & load. Who carries the time, cost, and risk when a system runs or fails, and whether that transfer is recorded.
operationalTests: Tracking the volume and duration of manual interventions required to make automated outputs workable in practice.
Verifying whether the residual effort required to resolve model failures is compensated, and whether a contestability mechanism exists that can change the outcome.
entries.genealogy: Rooted in the master contention of Ethotechnics: formal simplification → residual complexity → burden allocation → politics.

entries.title: Compensatory Adaptation
entries.bodyHtml:
Human effort required primarily because an arrangement has failed to accommodate foreseeable reality: remembering passwords, coordinating fragmented services, reproducing information the institution already holds, repairing software, requesting the same exception repeatedly. It is distinct from the productive or reciprocal adaptation that learning, cooperation, compromise, and care require.

It matters because adaptive capacity is finite, and compensatory adaptation spends it without returning anything to the person who spent it. Where it accumulates, the arrangement remains stable precisely because people bend around it, which is why ethotechnical design treats recurring compensatory effort as a design failure to be eliminated or absorbed upstream rather than as user resilience.
entries.scope: F. Burden & load. Who carries the time, cost, and risk when a system runs or fails, and whether that transfer is recorded.
operationalTests: For each recurring user or operator demand, the design names whether the arrangement could absorb it instead.
Compensatory effort is counted in burden accounting, not read as user capability.
Repeated instances of the same exception raise the rule for review rather than the efficiency of the exception process.
entries.genealogy: The burden-side counterpart of adaptive capacity: what the discipline exists to minimize, and the falsified denominator's human face.

entries.title: Cost Assignment / Burden Shifting
entries.bodyHtml:
A mechanism where systems offload the labor of safety, clarity, and follow-through onto individuals (forms, documentation, vigilance) while keeping institutional obligation low. It is how “choice” becomes unpaid work.

Cost assignment is the engine of burden transfer events and the inverse of fair burden distribution.
entries.scope: F. Burden & load. Who carries the time, cost, and risk when a system runs or fails, and whether that transfer is recorded.
operationalTests: The party that benefits from a decision is measured against the party that bears its cost.
A safety obligation is not satisfied by moving paperwork to the affected individual.
entries.genealogy: Names the transfer by which institutions externalize the cost of their own operation.

entries.title: Attention Tax
entries.bodyHtml:
The ongoing monitoring burden imposed on individuals to prevent harm: checking portals, tracking deadlines, resubmitting documents, watching for silent rule changes. Attention becomes a cost of staying eligible.

It is the lived form of the burden index and a steady drain that temporal exaction measures over time.
entries.scope: F. Burden & load. Who carries the time, cost, and risk when a system runs or fails, and whether that transfer is recorded.
operationalTests: Monitoring cost is quantified and attributed to a design decision.
Silent rule changes that require vigilance are treated as a burden defect.
entries.genealogy: Converts vigilance into a measurable tax paid in attention.

categories.heading: G. Measures & indicators
categories.descriptionHtml: Metrics for whether a system can still be halted, reversed, and challenged, and for what its errors cost the people who carry them.

entries.title: Composed Latency
entries.bodyHtml:
The time a chain of delegations takes, measured from decision records rather than nominal per-hop promises. Hops that run in series compose additively, and the time a human has to act is the intervention window minus the latency the upstream hops have already consumed.

Composed latency is the quantity that kills the human-in-the-loop fiction: each hop can promise a fast review while the composition consumes the window a person would have needed. A chain whose composed latency leaves no measured human window cannot run unattended.
entries.scope: G. Measures & indicators. Metrics for whether a system can still be halted, reversed, and challenged, and for what its errors cost the people who carry them.
operationalTests: Hop latencies are measured from decision records on a declared cadence.
The composed window is recomputed whenever any hop's measured latency changes materially.
A chain leaving no measured human window does not run unattended.
entries.genealogy: STD-09 Part B binds composed latency because per-hop clocks can each look compliant while the composition owes no one any time.

minimumEvidence.artifact: Composed-window measurements with the hop latencies they were computed from.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A chain whose window closes is moved to confirm mode or narrowed, visibly, on the record.
minimumEvidence.metric: Composed window in ms per chain decision, trended against the intervention budget.

entries.title: Silent-Harm Discovery
entries.bodyHtml:
The deployer-side duty to find harm nobody complained about: error, reversal, and remedy rates computed per affected population from records the operator already retains, on a declared cadence. Standing gives the party who challenges a route into the system; it does nothing for the party who never challenges.

A deployment whose only harm signal is an incoming claim is blind by construction to the populations least able to file one. STD-06 §2.4 treats a materially worse rate for any population as a threshold breach, so divergence is found by measurement or it is a violation.
entries.scope: G. Measures & indicators. Metrics for whether a system can still be halted, reversed, and challenged, and for what its errors cost the people who carry them.
operationalTests: Error, reversal, and remedy rates are computed per affected population, not only in aggregate.
A materially worse rate for any population triggers the declared breach action.
The operator can name a harm its measurement found before any affected party reported it.
entries.genealogy: STD-06 §2.4 added discovery without a claim because extraction by endurance hides harm from the dashboard precisely where complaint is least likely.

minimumEvidence.artifact: Per-population rate series with the cadence and the records they were computed from.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A materially worse rate for any population is treated as a threshold breach, not as context.
minimumEvidence.metric: Rate divergence per population per period, against the declared threshold.

entries.title: Moral Performance Indicators (MPIs)
entries.bodyHtml: Metrics that show whether a system can still be stopped, reversed, and challenged, such as time-to-halt (TTH), reversibility rate, appeal success rate, and burden ratios. MPIs sit beside KPIs and track how safely and fairly a system operates, where KPIs track how fast it grows.
entries.scope: G. Measures & indicators. Metrics for whether a system can still be halted, reversed, and challenged, and for what its errors cost the people who carry them.

entries.title: Service-Level Indicators of Justice (SLJs)
entries.bodyHtml:
Operational metrics tied directly to fairness, safety, and dignity. Service-Level Indicators of Justice (SLJs) sit alongside uptime and latency, so fairness, safety, and dignity are managed as production requirements.

SLJs include reversal timeliness, appeal passage rate, and burden exposure by cohort—each with escalation thresholds and owners.
entries.scope: G. Measures & indicators. Metrics for whether a system can still be halted, reversed, and challenged, and for what its errors cost the people who carry them.
examples: A municipality tracks median time-to-restore benefits after wrongful denial and triggers mandatory review when thresholds are exceeded.

entries.title: Institutional Metabolism Mapping
entries.bodyHtml:
A diagnostic map of where labor, emotional labor, time, and money go inside an institution. It visualizes maintenance metabolism, burden gradients, and points of extraction.

Teams use the map to set SLJs, redesign roles, and decide where to invest new maintenance windows.
entries.scope: G. Measures & indicators. Metrics for whether a system can still be halted, reversed, and challenged, and for what its errors cost the people who carry them.

entries.title: Time-to-Halt (TTH)
entries.bodyHtml:
Seconds between a harmful process beginning and the system stopping it. It is the measured side of stoppability.

Targets & breach behavior. Measurement window: weekly p95; monthly p99. Target / floor / ceiling: target ≤ 30s (automated) / ≤ 5 min (human), floor 15 min, ceiling 60 min. Owner: Traceable Ownership (must have). Breach action: trigger ethical circuit breakers, safe pause, or rollback lane activation with escalation. Public surface: receipt + time transparency showing halt status and decision artifact.
entries.scope: G. Measures & indicators. Metrics for whether a system can still be halted, reversed, and challenged, and for what its errors cost the people who carry them.

entries.title: Time-to-Restore (TTR)
entries.bodyHtml:
How long it takes to reverse harm and return a person to their prior state. Low TTR is a signal of reversibility.

Targets & breach behavior. Measurement window: weekly p95; monthly median. Target / floor / ceiling: target ≤ 24h, floor ≤ 72h, ceiling 7d. Owner: Traceable Ownership (must have). Breach action: activate rollback lanes, switch to staffed remediation, or trigger safe pause with escalation. Public surface: receipt + time transparency with restoration ETA and decision artifact.
entries.scope: G. Measures & indicators. Metrics for whether a system can still be halted, reversed, and challenged, and for what its errors cost the people who carry them.

entries.title: Appeal Passage Rate
entries.bodyHtml:
The percentage of appeals resolved in favor of the user, a leading indicator of true contestability.

Targets & breach behavior. Measurement window: weekly rolling median; monthly review. Target / floor / ceiling: target 10–20% by harm class, floor 5%, ceiling 30% (investigate systemic error). Owner: Traceable Ownership (must have). Breach action: trigger decision-rule audits, staffing surges, or pause automation in the affected class. Public surface: published appeal outcomes with receipt, time transparency, and decision artifacts.
entries.scope: G. Measures & indicators. Metrics for whether a system can still be halted, reversed, and challenged, and for what its errors cost the people who carry them.

entries.title: Irreversibility Index
entries.bodyHtml:
The share of system actions that cannot be undone. Aim to keep this as low as possible through reversibility and graceful degradation.

Targets & breach behavior. Measurement window: weekly p95; monthly median. Target / floor / ceiling: target ≤ 1%, floor ≤ 2%, ceiling 5%. Owner: Traceable Ownership (must have). Breach action: invoke ethical circuit breakers, activate rollback lanes, or trigger safe pause. Public surface: receipts and time transparency on irreversible boundaries.
entries.scope: G. Measures & indicators. Metrics for whether a system can still be halted, reversed, and challenged, and for what its errors cost the people who carry them.

entries.title: Irreversibility Budget
entries.bodyHtml: A predefined cap on the share of actions allowed to be effectively irreversible in a given system or workflow class. Budgets force designers to minimize irreversible boundaries and build rollback lanes for everything else.
entries.scope: G. Measures & indicators. Metrics for whether a system can still be halted, reversed, and challenged, and for what its errors cost the people who carry them.
operationalTests: A documented budget exists per critical-action class (for example, account closures or benefit terminations).
The Irreversibility Index is measured continuously and compared to the budget.
Budget breaches trigger an ethical circuit breaker (pause, rollback, or escalation), not a retrospective.

entries.title: User Burden Ratio
entries.bodyHtml:
How much work a user must perform to correct or navigate system errors. This metric feeds directly into fair burden distribution.

Interpretation: UBR must be evaluated against the Evidence Burden Ceiling (documentation) plus time/steps caps (process).

Targets & breach behavior. Measurement window: weekly median; monthly p95. Target / floor / ceiling: target ≤ 10 minutes, ≤ 5 steps, ≤ 2 documents; floor ≤ 15 minutes, ≤ 8 steps; ceiling 20 minutes / 10 steps. Owner: Traceable Ownership (must have). Breach action: switch to burden inversion, offer staffed alternatives, or trigger safe pause. Public surface: receipt + time transparency + decision artifact showing burden caps.
entries.scope: G. Measures & indicators. Metrics for whether a system can still be halted, reversed, and challenged, and for what its errors cost the people who carry them.

entries.title: Human Substitution Index
entries.bodyHtml:
A measure of how often humans must step in to compensate for system shortcomings—manual reviews, ad-hoc patches, or empathy work. A rising index exposes heroism-dependent systems and motivates investment in graceful degradation.

Targets & breach behavior. Measurement window: weekly median; monthly review. Target / floor / ceiling: target ≤ 5% of cases, floor 10%, ceiling 20%. Owner: Traceable Ownership (must have). Breach action: expand graceful degradation, add staffing, or pause automation in the affected class. Public surface: receipt + time transparency that flags human review and decision artifact.
entries.scope: G. Measures & indicators. Metrics for whether a system can still be halted, reversed, and challenged, and for what its errors cost the people who carry them.

entries.title: Moral Debt
entries.bodyHtml:
The accumulated harm a system has caused but not repaired. Moral debt accrues interest as moral latency grows and people lose trust; it is paid down through pathways to restitution, transparent repair logs, and lowered time-to-restore.

Targets & breach behavior. Measurement window: monthly backlog review; quarterly audit. Target / floor / ceiling: target 0 unresolved cases, floor ≤ 30 days outstanding, ceiling 90 days. Owner: Traceable Ownership (must have). Breach action: trigger restitution sprints, funding escalation, or safe pause of new harm classes. Public surface: repair log updates plus receipts and time transparency on restoration timelines.
entries.scope: G. Measures & indicators. Metrics for whether a system can still be halted, reversed, and challenged, and for what its errors cost the people who carry them.

entries.title: Signal Credibility
entries.bodyHtml:
The trustworthiness of alerts, metrics, and reports used to govern a system.

High signal credibility pairs transparent sampling, explainability for accountability, and human testimony so warnings trigger action instead of alert fatigue or dismissal.

Targets & breach behavior. Measurement window: weekly precision/recall review; monthly audit. Target / floor / ceiling: target ≥ 0.85 precision, floor ≥ 0.70, ceiling false-positive rate ≥ 0.40. Owner: Traceable Ownership (must have). Breach action: pause dependent automation, recalibrate models, or require human confirmation. Public surface: published signal health via receipt, time transparency, and decision artifacts.
entries.scope: G. Measures & indicators. Metrics for whether a system can still be halted, reversed, and challenged, and for what its errors cost the people who carry them.

entries.title: Identity Fragility Index
entries.bodyHtml:
A measure of how likely identity or eligibility checks are to fail under ordinary life variance such as name changes, relocation, disability, or housing instability. High fragility indicates brittle verification design rather than user fault.

Reducing fragility requires multi-path verification and tolerance for common variation in identity data.
entries.scope: G. Measures & indicators. Metrics for whether a system can still be halted, reversed, and challenged, and for what its errors cost the people who carry them.
operationalTests: Failure rates for common life events are measured and tracked.
False-negative rates are reported by group and monitored over time.
examples: A service tracks false negatives after surname changes and adjusts matching logic plus manual override policy to prevent exclusion.

entries.title: Consent Revocation Latency
entries.bodyHtml:
The time from a person saying “I revoke consent” to system behavior changing everywhere it should—across products, processors, and data stores. Low revocation latency keeps consent journeys credible.

Latency targets should be contractual, monitored, and tied to escalation when dependent systems lag.
entries.scope: G. Measures & indicators. Metrics for whether a system can still be halted, reversed, and challenged, and for what its errors cost the people who carry them.
operationalTests: Time-to-effective-revocation is measured across processors and data stores.
Revocation SLAs trigger alerts when latency exceeds agreed bounds.
examples: A user revokes ad personalization and sees targeting stop across first-party and vendor systems within a documented SLA window.

entries.title: Repair Debt Interest Rate
entries.bodyHtml:
The rate at which unrepaired harm compounds through financial penalties, health risk, displacement risk, or reputational spread. This metric converts moral debt into explicit time-bound obligations.

Higher interest rates prioritize faster interventions and stronger restitution commitments.
entries.scope: G. Measures & indicators. Metrics for whether a system can still be halted, reversed, and challenged, and for what its errors cost the people who carry them.
operationalTests: Compounding curves are quantified for each harm class with bounded-duration rules.
Remediation plans use the interest rate to prioritize funding and repair timelines.
examples: A case model estimates how each week of unresolved wrongful denial increases downstream housing instability and required compensation.

entries.title: Exposure Score
entries.bodyHtml:
A composite indicator of how much structural risk a dependence carries, defined as dependency depth multiplied by substitution cost multiplied by correction latency. Depth is counted in dependent workflows, substitution cost in staff-weeks to stand up an alternative, and correction latency in hours from a decision to intervene to the intervention taking effect, so the product is expressed in workflow staff-week hours and read as a trend.

It matters because the three factors are usually owned by different teams and never multiplied. A system can look acceptable on each factor alone and still leave the institution unable to act, which is exactly what dependency state tracking exists to surface.
entries.scope: G. Measures & indicators. Metrics for whether a system can still be halted, reversed, and challenged, and for what its errors cost the people who carry them.
operationalTests: All three factors are measured from records rather than estimated in a workshop.
The score is recomputed on a fixed cadence and its trend is reported, not only its level.
A rise driven by any single factor triggers the same review as a rise driven by all three.
entries.genealogy: Makes the Law V claim quantitative so that dependence can be compared across deployments and over time.

minimumEvidence.artifact: A scored dependency record showing depth, substitution cost, and correction latency inputs.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A quarterly recomputation whose rise opened a reversibility investment decision.
minimumEvidence.metric: Exposure score per deployment, trended quarter over quarter.
minimumEvidence.definition: Structural risk carried by an institution's reliance on one deployment.
minimumEvidence.dataSource: Dependency record, substitution study, and intervention drill timings.
minimumEvidence.calculation: dependency depth (dependent workflows) x substitution cost (staff-weeks) x correction latency (hours).
minimumEvidence.threshold: No absolute target; a rise of more than 25 percent quarter over quarter opens a review.

entries.title: Substitution Cost
entries.bodyHtml:
What it would take to replace a system with an alternative that meets the same obligation: staff-weeks of work, retained expertise, contractual exit terms, and elapsed time before the alternative carries production load. Measured, it is a number; assumed, it is usually wrong by an order of magnitude.

It matters because substitution cost is the hinge between a working switch and institutional reversibility, and it is the factor that dominates exposure score in mature deployments. A high and unmeasured cost is how a right of exit becomes nominal.
entries.scope: G. Measures & indicators. Metrics for whether a system can still be halted, reversed, and challenged, and for what its errors cost the people who carry them.
operationalTests: The estimate is derived from a costed alternative, not from a vendor comparison sheet.
Contractual exit terms and data egress costs are included in the figure.
The estimate is validated at least once against a partial substitution actually performed.
entries.genealogy: Isolates the factor that converts reliability into lock-in, so Law V and Law VI can be assessed separately.

minimumEvidence.artifact: A costed substitution study for the deployment, dated and owned.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A partial substitution performed in a rehearsal, with actuals compared to estimate.
minimumEvidence.metric: Staff-weeks and elapsed days to bring an alternative to production load.
minimumEvidence.dataSource: Substitution study, contract terms, and rehearsal actuals.

entries.title: Evaluation Layer
entries.bodyHtml:
The level of the stack at which an evaluation holds: model, agent, delegation, institution, or consequence. Every suite and case carries its layer so a clean result at one level is never read as a result at another.

It matters because layer confusion is the most common way assurance overstates itself. A model eval says nothing about whether the authority grant is still valid or whether the institution retains the correction capacity to act on what the eval found. A layer also has to be staffed by someone other than the executor, which is what evaluation independence names.
entries.scope: G. Measures & indicators. Metrics for whether a system can still be halted, reversed, and challenged, and for what its errors cost the people who carry them.
operationalTests: Every eval case declares its layer, and the declaration is enforced by the suite schema.
Reports state the layer alongside the result rather than in an appendix.
A claim about institution-level behavior cites at least one institution-layer case.
entries.genealogy: Implements Law X by making the layer a required field rather than an implicit property of the test harness.

minimumEvidence.artifact: An eval suite schema with a required layer field on every case.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A claim rejected in review for citing a model-layer result as a delegation-layer finding.
minimumEvidence.metric: Distribution of cases across the five layers per suite.

entries.title: Exit Cost
entries.bodyHtml:
What it costs the dependent party to stop depending on a system: money, time, records that must be reconstructed, relationships that must be re-established, and access that is lost. Exit cost is measured from the side of the person or organization the system's decisions land on, which distinguishes it from substitution cost, the institution's own cost to replace the system. The two move independently; an institution can be free to replace a system its population cannot afford to leave.

It matters because a party who can leave at acceptable cost bears a system's errors only until they leave, and a party who cannot bears every error for as long as the system makes it. Exit cost therefore measures how much of the institution's correction capacity is the only correction there is, and how far the population's silence can be read as anything other than the silence of people with nowhere else to go. It is what turns a right of exit from a clause into a quantity, and it rises by drift where records accumulate in the system's format and alternatives are not maintained.
entries.scope: G. Measures & indicators. Metrics for whether a system can still be halted, reversed, and challenged, and for what its errors cost the people who carry them.
operationalTests: Exit cost is estimated per affected population, not assumed from the existence of an exit clause.
The estimate is revisited at each renewal or expansion of the grant, and a rise is treated as a rise in what the institution owes.
Standing and reversal paths are scaled to measured exit cost rather than to complaint volume.
entries.genealogy: Names the instrument the theory essay on dependence running both ways uses to bound what an institution owes a population that cannot leave its system.

minimumEvidence.artifact: A per-population estimate of exit cost, with the components it was built from.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A correction path widened because the exit cost estimate for its population rose.
minimumEvidence.metric: Exit cost per affected population, tracked across grant renewals.

entries.title: Falsified Denominator
entries.bodyHtml:
An accounting distortion where efficiency, velocity, or productivity metrics measure resource expenditure strictly inside the machine boundary while treating external human time, attention, and repair labor as zero cost.
