By omitting externalized human absorption from the denominator, the institution manufactures an illusion of dramatic operational efficiency.

A system that takes 50 milliseconds of server time but requires 45 minutes of human troubleshooting across phone trees and manual appeal queues is not fast; it has falsified its denominator. Refusing the falsified denominator is the core demand of Axiom 1 (Finitude) and STD-01 (Temporal Rights). The general form is the falsified ledger: a boundary that excludes the costs, burdens, and failures needed to understand performance makes accurate accounting inside it produce a false account.
entries.scope: G. Measures & indicators. Metrics for whether a system can still be halted, reversed, and challenged, and for what its errors cost the people who carry them.
operationalTests: Comparing total end-to-end task resolution time (including user and operator labor) against server-side processing latency.
Confirming whether time spent on dispute resolution, appeals, and workarounds is budgeted and reported in operational dashboards.
entries.genealogy: Formulated to challenge technocratic productivity claims by accounting for human temporal extraction.

entries.title: Challenge Density
entries.bodyHtml:
The rate at which challenges arrive against the capacity to answer them. Per case, procedural force is a bounded transaction; in aggregate it is a budget line, and no institutional design survives refusing to do arithmetic. A response apparatus that is saturated is measuring the gap between the volume of error a system emits and the corrective capacity its delegation was granted with.

It matters because congestion is the point where the open circuit is usually lost. The reflexive response to volume is narrowing standing, which converts the open circuit back into a closed one exactly when the volume proves the system fails often. Density is governed by capacity decisions or scope decisions, not by eligibility decisions: sustained breaches of response clocks are a resourcing event, and an institution that meets them by narrowing who may challenge has treated a capacity signal as a permissions problem.
entries.scope: G. Measures & indicators. Metrics for whether a system can still be halted, reversed, and challenged, and for what its errors cost the people who carry them.
operationalTests: Challenge volume and response capacity are reported as a ratio, not as separate unread series.
A sustained breach of response clocks triggers a recorded resourcing or scope decision.
Standing was not narrowed, and no admissibility bar was raised, in direct response to a congestion breach.
entries.genealogy: Carries Law VII's per-case rule into the aggregate: the theory essay on challenge density answers the vetocracy objection with measured response capacity rather than narrower standing.

minimumEvidence.artifact: A challenge load series: volume, response capacity, and unanswered-challenge age, reported together.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A congestion breach answered with a resourcing or scope decision that is recorded and dated.
minimumEvidence.metric: Median challenge response latency and the age of the oldest unanswered challenge.

entries.title: Recourse Performance
entries.bodyHtml: How well a system delivers review → reversal → remedy under realistic load and stress. It composes time-to-halt, time-to-restore, and appeal passage rate into a single posture.
entries.scope: G. Measures & indicators. Metrics for whether a system can still be halted, reversed, and challenged, and for what its errors cost the people who carry them.
operationalTests: Recourse metrics are measured under realistic load, not only in the happy path.
A recourse failure is treated as a system defect with an owner and a fix date.
entries.genealogy: Folds the individual indicators into one end-to-end performance question.

entries.title: Reversal Cost
entries.bodyHtml:
The time, money, emotional labor, documentation, and social risk required to undo an outcome. High reversal cost makes errors durable and turns “rights” into luxuries.

It is the practical face of irreversibility and the target that a reversal SLA is meant to bound.
entries.scope: G. Measures & indicators. Metrics for whether a system can still be halted, reversed, and challenged, and for what its errors cost the people who carry them.
operationalTests: The cost to reverse a decision is quantified and capped.
A reversal that costs more than the harm it corrects is flagged as a design failure.
entries.genealogy: Prices the frictional barrier between a wrong state and its correction.

entries.title: Durability of Error
entries.bodyHtml:
How long a wrong state persists once created, and how far it propagates (downstream systems, eligibility, reputation). A system is dangerous when it can create durable errors quickly but correct them slowly.

It is what error cascades amplify and what moral latency measures between harm and correction.
entries.scope: G. Measures & indicators. Metrics for whether a system can still be halted, reversed, and challenged, and for what its errors cost the people who carry them.
operationalTests: The lifetime of a wrong state is measured from creation to correction.
Propagation paths are mapped so an error’s downstream blast radius is known.
entries.genealogy: Makes error persistence a first-class safety metric rather than a footnote.

entries.title: Dual-Ledger Evaluation
entries.bodyHtml:
A dual-ledger evaluation is an assessment framework that pairs visible operational metrics (resolution speed, unit cost, throughput) with an independent audit ledger measuring human capacity depletion, uncounted compensatory labor, and contestation standing.

Under dual-ledger scoring, non-compensatory floors prevent high visible output from offsetting failures on human depletion or suppressed rights.
examples: An AI triage audit calculates visible diagnostic speed on one ledger and nursing overtime and burnout risk on an independent audit ledger.
entries.scope: G. Measures & indicators. Metrics for whether a system can still be halted, reversed, and challenged, and for what its errors cost the people who carry them.
operationalTests: Evaluation reports present both operational throughput and independent audit metrics with non-compensatory scoring floors.
A high score on processing speed cannot offset an audit finding of unrecorded compensatory human labor.
entries.genealogy: Adapted from double-entry bookkeeping and environmental economics to prevent unmeasured externalities in automated system audits.

categories.heading: H. Governance & power
categories.descriptionHtml: Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.

entries.title: Attestation
entries.bodyHtml:
The signature binding a record to a named key holder at a point in time. An attestation carries the key-holder identifier, the algorithm, the signature, and when it was produced, so that authority that cannot be attributed to a key holder is distinguishable from authority nobody signed.

It matters because delegation otherwise becomes orphaned: capability exercises the authority and no one answers for it. An attestation older than the record's last transition covers a record that no longer exists, so re-attestation at renewal is part of the discipline rather than a courtesy.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
operationalTests: Every authority grant carries signed_by, algorithm, signature, and signed_at.
A signature older than the last state transition is reported as stale, not current.
The payload digest reproduces the exact signed content.
entries.genealogy: STD-08 added the attestation to the authority grant so that the Liability Record answers who answers for a delegation and the attestation answers who put it in force.

minimumEvidence.artifact: Grant records carrying attestation blocks with key holder, algorithm, and signed_at.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A grant whose signature predates its last state transition is refused as evidence of the current state.
minimumEvidence.metric: Share of live grants whose attestation is newer than their last transition.

entries.title: Liability Record
entries.bodyHtml:
The object on an authority grant naming the party that accepts liability for the latency and errors of the automation, the instrument that binds them, and the carve-outs they claim. It exists because a system may not hide behind algorithmic error: the operating institution answers for what its delegation does.

Carve-outs are recorded before an incident rather than assembled after one. A limitation the issuer knows about is priced at deployment; the record exists so the residual risk everyone else carries is visible in the issuer's words, not the defendant's.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
operationalTests: Every grant names the party accepting liability and the instrument that binds them.
Carve-outs, caps, and exclusions appear on the record, not in a dispute.
Sub-contracting does not diffuse liability: the head grant answers for every hop of a chain.
entries.genealogy: STD-01 §6.2 states the liability of automata; STD-08 gave the statement an object so the acceptance is inspectable rather than assumed.

minimumEvidence.artifact: Grant records with a liability object naming accepting party, instrument, and carve-outs.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A deployment with no recorded liability acceptance does not pass its safety-case review.
minimumEvidence.metric: Share of consequential grants with a named liability party and a recorded instrument.

entries.title: Carve-Out
entries.bodyHtml:
An exclusion, cap, or condition the accepting party claims against a recorded liability. Carve-outs are recorded on the liability record rather than reserved for litigation, because the forensically useful moment to assemble an excuse is before the harm, in the issuer's words.

A carve-out on the record is a price: it states how much of the risk the liability does not cover and therefore who carries the rest. A carve-out that surfaces for the first time in a dispute is evidence of concealment rather than a term of the deal.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
operationalTests: Every carve-out claimed against a liability appears on the grant record.
The residual risk a carve-out leaves is identifiable and priced.
No carve-out appears first in a dispute.
entries.genealogy: STD-08 records carve-outs as part of the liability object so the excuse is assembled before the incident.

minimumEvidence.artifact: Liability records listing every claimed exclusion or cap with its basis.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A dispute resolved by invoking a carve-out that was never recorded counts as a governance failure.
minimumEvidence.metric: Count of carve-outs per liability record and their aggregate coverage gap.

entries.title: Delegation Chain
entries.bodyHtml:
A sequence of delegations that together produce one consequential decision: an agent sub-contracting to an agent, a service calling a service, across components, providers, or institutions. STD-09's claim is that the chain is itself a delegation, governed at the layer where it fails: enumerated hops on the head grant, liability terminating at the head, one intervention at the boundary.

Each hop can satisfy the standards alone while the composition remains unauditable and attributed to no one. The chain exists as an object so it can be paused, challenged, and attributed as one delegation rather than as a pile of conformant parts.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
operationalTests: The head grant enumerates every contributing delegation in execution order.
Every hop resolves to a full grant with its own scope, mode, and revocation conditions.
One intervention at the boundary halts every hop, with a receipt for the chain.
entries.genealogy: STD-09 exists because per-hop conformance does not compose: the relevant eval sits at the highest layer where harm can emerge, and for a chain that layer is the chain.

minimumEvidence.artifact: Head grants with a chain field resolving to full grant records per hop.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A boundary intervention halts every hop and emits one chain-level halt receipt.
minimumEvidence.metric: Share of consequential decisions whose chain is fully enumerated.

entries.title: Design Authority
entries.bodyHtml: The accountable power to set the constraints a system operates under, choose its safeguards, and fund their enforcement. Clear design authority aligns incentives, protects contestability, and prevents accountability diffusion.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.

entries.title: Oversight Horizon
entries.bodyHtml: The distance regulators, auditors, or affected communities can see into a system’s decisions and their effects. Extending the horizon through harm visibility, traceable models, and shared repair logs shrinks dead zones.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.

entries.title: Permission Surface
entries.bodyHtml:
The set of authority grants in force for a system at a given moment, each carrying an evidence basis, a scope, a state, and an expiry. The surface is described by authority rather than by access points: an unused grant is still part of it, and a reachable capability with no grant behind it is not part of it at all.

Every element of the surface is an authority grant that can be narrowed, suspended, or allowed to lapse, which is what makes the surface governable rather than merely documented. Comparing the surface against the capability catalog is the direct test of whether capability has outrun permission, and a wide surface makes contestability practical only when each grant in it can be challenged.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
examples: A tenant can pause automated collections, download their case record, and request human review without manager pre-approval.

entries.title: Bounded Autonomy
entries.bodyHtml:
Autonomy granted only within explicit limits; approaching or crossing those limits must trigger escalation to design authority or a documented oversight horizon.

The limits live in an authority grant and are enforced through its grant state. Widening them is an expansion decision, not a configuration change.
examples: A claims assistant can approve payouts up to $500, but anything higher is routed to a supervisor.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.

entries.title: Earned Autonomy
entries.bodyHtml:
Autonomy that expands only after demonstrated reliability, monitoring, and accountability. Permission surfaces widen as traceable ownership and repair logs prove the system can handle more scope.

The demonstration is evidence for widening a specific authority grant, recorded as a transition in its grant state. Reliability is the argument for an expansion decision, never a substitute for one.
examples: After six months of clean audits, the escalation bot gains approval rights for low-risk cases.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.

entries.title: Scope Discipline
entries.bodyHtml: The practice of not exceeding one’s mandate, even when doing so might appear helpful or efficient. Scope discipline enforces the permission surface and respects bounded autonomy.
examples: A support bot refuses to access customer data outside its assigned ticket.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.

entries.title: Right of Exit
entries.bodyHtml:
The ability to leave a system without ruinous cost, retaliation, or silent lock-in. Consent means little when departure is punitive, so right of exit is a precondition for consent.

Operationally, exit requires data portability, clear closure paths, and protections against downstream penalties.

Exit is real only when it is priced. A measured substitution cost and demonstrated institutional reversibility are what separate a right of exit from a clause nobody can afford to invoke. Consent depth is the reason the pricing has to be redone: the choice made at adoption was not a choice about the dependency that grew afterwards.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
examples: Workers can opt out of an automated scheduling tool and keep equivalent access to shifts while a manual process remains available.

entries.title: Externalized Harm Channels
entries.bodyHtml:
The pathways through which institutions push risk, cleanup, or delay onto others: contractors, users, bystanders, or future teams. Mapping these channels exposes hidden transfer mechanisms behind nominally efficient systems.

The map is used to give each channel an accountable owner and to move the burden back toward the system owner.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
examples: A platform offloads fraud remediation to merchants without funding support capacity, shifting investigation labor downstream.

entries.title: Stewardship Window
entries.bodyHtml:
A negotiated period where teams pause growth work to do maintenance, close open repairs, and fix gaps in ownership.

Stewardship windows bundle maintenance windows, publish SLJs for the pause, and commit to closing items in the repair log before resuming throughput.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.

entries.title: Stewardship
entries.bodyHtml: An explicit, ongoing role responsible for system behavior over time, with authority to pause, fix, or retire it. Stewardship links design authority, stoppability, and stewardship windows.
examples: A named steward can pause a rollout and own the repair log.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.

entries.title: Governance by Suspension
entries.bodyHtml:
Control exercised by keeping matters unresolved long enough that time itself produces the outcome.

Governance by suspension relies on non-decisions and exploits endurance asymmetry.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.

entries.title: Endurance Asymmetry
entries.bodyHtml:
Institutions can persist indefinitely; humans cannot. This makes delay an allocation mechanism.

Endurance asymmetry underwrites continuity privilege and punitive friction.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.

entries.title: Continuity Privilege
entries.bodyHtml:
Unequal access to enforceability produced by unequal capacity to maintain standing over time (attention, health, documentation, slack).

Continuity privilege steepens the burden gradient for those without reserves.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.

entries.title: Proxy Privilege
entries.bodyHtml:
Unequal enforceability produced by unequal ability to delegate persistence (agents, intermediaries, automation).

Proxy privilege lets some parties bypass the futility threshold that others face alone.

The asymmetry becomes legible when each proxy holds a named authority grant with a visible grant state, so extending a proxy’s reach is an expansion decision rather than an unremarked advantage.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.

entries.title: Latency-as-Action
entries.bodyHtml:
The principle that delay produced predictably by system rules (queues, resets, blocked escalation, absent deadlines) is attributable power, not mere inaction.

Latency-as-action frames delay as governance and grounds decision artifacts.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.

entries.title: Bounded Duration
entries.bodyHtml:
A fixed maximum time-to-resolution; breach triggers an enforceable disposition.

Bounded duration pairs with a stable clock and time transparency.

Minimum evidence

  • User-facing artifact.
  • Internal log.
  • Drill / rehearsal.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.

entries.title: Continuity of State
entries.bodyHtml:
A persistent cumulative case record that prevents forced repetition of validated inputs across channels, time, and teams. Continuity of state lowers administrative burden and reduces avoidable denial loops.

It protects contestability by ensuring prior evidence remains legible during escalation or transfer.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
examples: A claimant can move from chat to phone support without re-uploading documents because prior verification artifacts follow the case.

entries.title: Safe Pause / Status Quo During Pendency
entries.bodyHtml:
No adverse consequences while review is pending (except narrow, reviewable emergency exception).

Safe pause preserves the utility window and keeps people whole during appeal.

Minimum evidence

  • User-facing artifact.
  • Internal log.
  • Drill / rehearsal.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
commonCounterfeits: “We won’t punish you” while consequences quietly accrue.

entries.title: Traceable Ownership
entries.bodyHtml:
A named responsible party with authority to override automation when bounds are breached.

Traceable ownership clarifies design authority and accelerates time-to-restore.

Minimum evidence

  • User-facing artifact.
  • Internal log.
  • Drill / rehearsal.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
commonCounterfeits: Team inbox or triage queue with no override authority.

entries.title: Time Transparency
entries.bodyHtml:
Legible process state: current step, blocking condition, time remaining, next decision point, escalation triggers; no fake progress.

Time transparency supports contestability and a stable clock.

Minimum evidence

  • User-facing artifact.
  • Internal log.
  • Drill / rehearsal.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
commonCounterfeits: “Status updates” with no time remaining or escalation triggers.

entries.title: Obligation Continuity
entries.bodyHtml:
Whether responsibility stays attached across time, handoffs, and narrative resets instead of evaporating.

Obligation continuity depends on traceable ownership, continuity of state, and a durable repair log.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.

entries.title: Delay as Power
entries.bodyHtml:
The ability to remain wrong without consequence by stretching time (“pending,” “in review”).

Delay as power operationalizes latency-as-action and shows up in governance by suspension.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.

entries.title: Performance-Gated Remedy
entries.bodyHtml:
The correction path works only if someone performs well under stress; the system treats composure as eligibility.

Performance-gated remedy undermines contestability and violates care floor guarantees.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.

entries.title: Bindingness After Contact
entries.bodyHtml:
After harm is reported or help is requested, who becomes bound—institution or claimant—and what obligations lock in.

Bindingness after contact requires traceable ownership and a time-bounded repair log.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.

entries.title: Recognition as Solvent
entries.bodyHtml:
Being “heard” is treated as if it discharges obligation, pressuring the claimant to stop escalating without repair.

Recognition as solvent swaps procedural empathy for material pathways to restitution.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.

entries.title: Unowned Obligation
entries.bodyHtml:
Responsibility exists but no owner or time-bound state transition is attached; people are bounced between channels.

Unowned obligation signals missing traceable ownership and weak bounded duration.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.

entries.title: Closure-Code Regime
entries.bodyHtml:
The set of person-level reason codes that convert structural scarcity into individual failure (“withdrew,” “no response,” “noncompliant”).

Closure-code regimes mask governance by suspension and normalize punitive friction.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.

entries.title: Attrition-as-Resolution
entries.bodyHtml:
An anti-pattern where drop-off is counted as success and metrics improve when people give up. Attrition-as-resolution hides unmet obligations behind completion dashboards.

It often co-occurs with endurance asymmetry and extraction by endurance, shifting repair cost onto those with the least capacity.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
examples: A benefits workflow reports higher “closure” rates after adding extra verification loops that cause applicants to abandon appeals.

entries.title: Legitimacy Laundering
entries.bodyHtml:
Moral language (“we care,” “be reasonable”) substitutes for binding obligation and repair.

Legitimacy laundering offers recognition without bindingness after contact or a repair log.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.

entries.title: Legitimacy Engineering
entries.bodyHtml:
Legitimacy defined by stoppability, reversibility, contestability, ownership, and time-bounded repair capacity.

Legitimacy engineering centers stoppability, reversibility, and contestability as measurable requirements.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.

entries.title: Exit Coercion
entries.bodyHtml:
“Consent” and silence extracted under duress during departures, often via NDAs, retaliation risk, or narrative erasure.

Exit coercion violates the right of exit and collapses refusal budgets.

Coercion is easiest where leaving is expensive, so the countermeasures are the ones that make leaving affordable: a measured substitution cost and maintained institutional reversibility. Where neither is maintained, consent depth does the coercing on its own and no one has to apply pressure.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.

entries.title: Retaliation Surface
entries.bodyHtml: Where the system can punish people for contesting, pausing, refusing, or exiting—through throttling, stricter scrutiny, “account review,” or service withdrawal. Mapping the retaliation surface protects contestability and the right of exit.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
operationalTests: Teams can name every lever that can worsen a claimant’s state after an appeal is filed, including throttling, scrutiny, account review, or service withdrawal.
Safeguards document how retaliation levers are disabled or monitored during appeals.

entries.title: Non-Retaliation Guarantee
entries.bodyHtml: A binding commitment that contesting, pausing, refusing, or exiting will not trigger adverse treatment. A non-retaliation guarantee makes contestability and the right of exit safe to exercise.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
operationalTests: Adverse-action rates are tracked for users who appeal versus those who do not.
Policies and interfaces explicitly state that contesting, pausing, refusing, or exiting will not trigger adverse treatment.

entries.title: Appeal Integrity
entries.bodyHtml:
Appeals are judged on merits with transparent criteria, named authority, and documented outcomes—not absorbed into procedural theater. Appeal integrity ensures contestability yields real corrective action.

Strong integrity requires publishable decision artifacts, reversible outcomes, and safeguards against retaliatory handling.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
operationalTests: The share of appeals receiving a decision artifact is tracked and published.
Appeals include named authority with overturn power rather than advisory review only.
examples: An appeals dashboard shows overturn rate, rationale categories, and median response time by decision class.

entries.title: Escalation Reliability
entries.bodyHtml: Escalation paths work under load, after hours, and for novices, as shown in drills rather than in documentation. Reliable escalation keeps ethical load paths intact when stress is highest.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
operationalTests: Escalation drills hit time-to-human and time-to-decision targets across nights, weekends, and peak load.
Novice users can reach the same escalation path without privileged channels.

entries.title: Decision Reversal Authority
entries.bodyHtml:
A formally granted power to undo harmful decisions, not merely recommend reconsideration. Decision reversal authority turns reversibility into an enforceable capability with named ownership.

Authority should include scope boundaries, auditability, and response clocks so reversals can occur during live incidents.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
operationalTests: A named role has unilateral reversal power for defined classes of harm.
Policy and tooling document how reversals are executed and logged.
examples: A safety officer can immediately reverse automated account suspensions for urgent livelihood-impact cases without waiting for weekly review.

entries.title: Restitution Ladder
entries.bodyHtml: A tiered remedy system that moves from apology to reversal, compensation, repair service, and systemic fix triggers. The restitution ladder ensures pathways to restitution stay practical and selectable.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
operationalTests: The restitution ladder exists, is selectable in policy or tooling, and is routinely used.
Case reviews show remedies advancing beyond apologies when harm warrants compensation or repair services.

entries.title: Remedy Equivalence
entries.bodyHtml:
Manual and automated channels must offer equivalent remedy outcomes, timelines, and authority. People should not be penalized for choosing accessibility, safety, or human review paths.

Remedy equivalence is measured by comparing reversal rates, escalation success, and time-to-resolution across channels.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
operationalTests: Appeal passage rates and time-to-resolution are compared across manual and automated channels.
Policy guarantees that manual paths can reach the same remedy outcomes as automated paths.
examples: A disability accommodation appeal filed by phone has the same overturn authority and SLA as the web portal process.

entries.title: Case Ownership Continuity
entries.bodyHtml: Cases do not become orphaned across handoffs; ownership persists through vacations, organizational changes, or vendor transfers. Case ownership continuity strengthens traceable ownership for contested decisions.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
operationalTests: Cases never enter a “no owner” state, and ownership transitions are logged and visible.
Handoff procedures assign a new owner with backup coverage before the previous owner exits.

entries.title: Revisable Delegation
entries.bodyHtml:
Delegation of consequential work to a machine that stays tied to the evidence and beliefs that justified it, so the grant can be narrowed, suspended, or withdrawn when those change. A revisable delegation names its holder, its ceiling, what it depends on, and what would revoke it; an unrevisable one is a transfer with a delegation's name. The objects it is written in are the authority grant, the policy record it depends on, and the delegated agency the grant creates.

Revisability is the standing property. Justified delegation is the same coupling read in the present tense: whether authority, evidence, and correction capacity are all in force right now. The two are one question at two timescales. A delegation that is justified today but not revisable cannot act on tomorrow's answer.

The question it serves is how an institution can become more capable without becoming less revisable. The record shape is defined in STD-07, and the terms the delegation must keep meeting while it stands are in STD-08. The test is whether the institution can answer, for any past action, what it believed at the time, what it had authorized, and what has since changed.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
operationalTests: Every authorization record lists its revocation conditions and the beliefs it depends on.
A discrepancy that matches a revocation condition produces a revision within a declared clock.
Someone outside the system has standing to object, and the objection is answered on the record.
entries.genealogy: Ethotechnics uses Revisable Delegation to name the property that bounded autonomy, decision reversal authority, and meta-contestability jointly protect once an institution lets machines act on its behalf.

minimumEvidence.artifact: An authorization record carrying holder, ceiling, depends_on, and revocation conditions.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A delegation narrowed or withdrawn in response to a recorded discrepancy, with the chain visible.
minimumEvidence.metric: Time from a matching discrepancy to the revision that answers it, against the declared clock.

examples: An agent's standing deploy permission is tied to a verified staging check; when the check breaks, the permission drops to confirm-mode automatically and the log shows which record forced it.

entries.title: Authority Grant
entries.bodyHtml:
The record that permits a named holder to take a bounded class of actions, for whom, under what conditions, and until when. A grant carries its scope, its evidence basis, its grant state, its expiry, and the policy records it depends on.

It matters because authority that is not written as a record cannot be reviewed, narrowed, or withdrawn. A grant that carries its dependencies and its revocation conditions is what makes the delegation a revisable delegation rather than a transfer. The grant is what makes authority drift detectable rather than merely regrettable after the fact.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
operationalTests: Every action class a system may perform maps to exactly one grant with a named holder.
Each grant states an expiry and the conditions under which it is revoked.
A grant with no revocation conditions is flagged as a transfer rather than a delegation.
entries.genealogy: Ethotechnics separates the grant from the capability so that Law I, capability does not imply authority, has an object to bind to.

minimumEvidence.artifact: An authority grant register with holder, scope, state, evidence basis, and expiry.
minimumEvidence.behavior: An attempted action outside grant scope refused and logged with the grant id.
minimumEvidence.metric: Count of live grants and share carrying a non-null expiry.

entries.title: Authority Lease
entries.bodyHtml:
The stance that a grant of authority is held for a term against a renewable justification rather than owned outright. A lease expires by default, and continuing an authority grant requires fresh evidence rather than the absence of complaints.

It matters because silence is the most common renewal mechanism in practice. Treating authority as a lease forces justified delegation to be re-established on a clock, and it puts the burden of proof on the delegation rather than on the people questioning it.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
operationalTests: Every grant has a renewal date, and passing it changes the grant state without human action.
Renewal packets cite new evidence, not the original approval.
The renewal burden rises with the consequence class and the elapsed duration of the grant.
entries.genealogy: States Law II as a property relationship: authority is leasehold, and absence of observed failure is not payment of the rent.

minimumEvidence.artifact: A renewal record naming the evidence that justifies continuing the grant for a further term.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A grant lapsing on its renewal date because no renewal packet was filed.
minimumEvidence.metric: Median age of live grants against their declared renewal interval.

entries.title: Policy Record
entries.bodyHtml:
A versioned statement of the propositions a delegation rests on: what the model does, who the population is, what the downstream process catches, and when each claim expires. Grants cite policy records rather than restating their assumptions, which is what policy as state requires.

It matters because assumptions decay silently when they are held as launch documents. Held as a record with a version and an expiry, a policy can raise a review trigger and move a grant state when the world changes. That propagation is the mechanism behind a revisable delegation: the delegation narrows because a proposition it rested on lapsed.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
operationalTests: Each policy record states its assumptions, its evidence, its version, and its review date.
Grants reference policy records by id and version rather than paraphrasing them.
Passing a review date changes the record status and propagates to every grant that cites it.
entries.genealogy: Gives Law III an object: the propositions that justify a grant are stored where a change in the world can reach them.

minimumEvidence.artifact: A policy record with assumptions, evidence refs, version, and review date.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A lapsed policy record moving its dependent grants to review_required.
minimumEvidence.metric: Share of live grants whose cited policy records are all within their review dates.

entries.title: Review Trigger
entries.bodyHtml:
A declared rule connecting an observation to a state change: when this discrepancy, expiry, or threshold occurs, this grant moves to this state, answered by this owner, within this clock. Triggers are the wiring between monitoring and authority, and they are what give a policy record force over a grant state.

It matters because observation without a possible transition is theater. A trigger is the smallest object that makes a dashboard part of the control system rather than a record of what already happened, and it is how policy as state acquires force over a running system.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
operationalTests: Every monitored signal names the state it can change, or is marked explicitly as informational.
Each trigger names an owner and a response clock.
Silence past the clock is treated as a governance failure, not as a pending state.
entries.genealogy: Implements Law VIII: the test of an observation is whether it can change the governing state of the system.

minimumEvidence.artifact: A trigger table mapping signals to state transitions, owners, and clocks.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A monitored discrepancy producing a reconsideration record within its clock.
minimumEvidence.metric: Share of monitored signals with a declared state transition, and clock breach rate.

entries.title: Correction Obligation
entries.bodyHtml:
The duty an institution takes on when it delegates consequential action: to notice, stop, reverse, and repair what the delegate does. The obligation is created by the delegation itself, not by the first incident.

It matters because delegating action also delegates the ability to be wrong at scale. Stating the obligation alongside the authority grant is what makes a shortfall in correction capacity visible before it is needed rather than during an incident.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
operationalTests: Each grant states the corrections its holder owes: which harms, notified how, reversed by whom.
Correction obligations are reviewed whenever the grant's scope or population changes.
An obligation with no funded capacity behind it is recorded as an open governance risk.
entries.genealogy: States Law IV as an object attached to the grant, so correction is authorized at the same moment as action.

minimumEvidence.artifact: A correction obligation clause on each grant, naming harms, owners, and clocks.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A scope increase blocked until the matching correction obligation was resourced.
minimumEvidence.metric: Count of stated obligations without a funded capacity owner.

entries.title: Preserved Capacity
entries.bodyHtml:
An institutional capability deliberately maintained so the institution can still question, replace, or withdraw a system: retained expertise, a working manual path, independent records, a viable alternative supplier. Preserved capacities are named, owned, and funded even while idle, and they are kept honest by withdrawal rehearsal.

It matters because these are the first capacities efficiency removes. Their erosion is a governance event rather than a saving, since it is the mechanism by which a system consumes the conditions of its own contestability, destroys institutional reversibility, and ends in institutional capture. Registered capacities also decay quietly through capacity depreciation, which is why exercise dates rather than register entries are the evidence.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
operationalTests: Preserved capacities are listed with an owner and a budget line, separate from the system's own budget.
Any proposal that reduces one is reviewed as a governance change, not as an efficiency measure.
Each capacity is exercised on a cadence so that its continued existence is demonstrated.
entries.genealogy: Gives Law XII its object: the capacities an institution needs in order to question, replace, or withdraw a consequential system.

minimumEvidence.artifact: A preserved capacity register with owners, budget lines, and exercise dates.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A cost reduction rejected or amended because it would erode a preserved capacity.
minimumEvidence.metric: Share of registered capacities exercised within their declared interval.

entries.title: Corrective Standing
entries.bodyHtml:
The recognized capacity of an error-bearing party to initiate correction: to raise a challenge that must be received, answered by a named responder, judged against a stated standard, and able to change the system's state. Standing is proportional to exposure and carries procedural force rather than veto.

It matters because contestability without standing is a suggestion box. Standing is what converts the experience of harm into an event the governing system has to process, and it is operationalized by a standing mechanism.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
operationalTests: Standing is declared per decision class rather than granted informally on request.
A challenge from someone with standing produces a dated response from a named party.
At least one successful challenge in the period changed a policy or grant, not only an outcome.
entries.genealogy: States Law VII in its Method-scoped form: exposure generates standing, and standing is procedural force, not control over the institution.

minimumEvidence.artifact: A standing declaration per decision class, naming who may challenge what.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A challenge raised by an affected party that changed a grant or policy state.
minimumEvidence.metric: Share of challenges answered within clock, and share producing a state change.

entries.title: Standing Mechanism
entries.bodyHtml:
The apparatus that makes standing real: a register of who may challenge which decision classes, including error-bearing parties, plus the admissible evidence, the responder, the deadline, the standard of review, and the set of state transitions a successful challenge can produce.

It matters because corrective standing declared without a mechanism can be neither exercised nor audited. The mechanism is the part of contestability an auditor can inspect: named responders, real clocks, and recorded outcomes.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
operationalTests: The register, responder, deadline, and standard of review are published, not held internally.
The set of possible outcomes includes at least one that changes system state.
Non-retaliation is attested and monitored for the parties who use the mechanism.
entries.genealogy: The mechanism side of Law VII, and the amendment surface for STD-02 where standard of review and state transitions are added.

minimumEvidence.artifact: A published standing mechanism specification with register, responder, clock, and outcomes.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A challenge routed through the mechanism and answered by the named responder on time.
minimumEvidence.metric: Challenge volume, response-clock breach rate, and outcome distribution.

entries.title: Procedural Force
entries.bodyHtml:
The property of a challenge that obliges a response and can change a state, as distinct from a veto that stops action outright. A challenge with procedural force must be received, answered on a clock, and capable of producing a transition; it need not prevail.

It matters because the usual objection to standing is fear of veto. Procedural force is the narrower claim that keeps corrective standing workable, and it is the difference between contestability and consultation.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
operationalTests: Every challenge channel names what must happen on receipt and by when.
The possible outcomes are enumerated, and at least one is a state change rather than an explanation.
A challenge that is answered but produces no possible transition is recorded as consultation.
entries.genealogy: Draws the line Law VII draws: standing is procedural force, not veto, so the claim survives contact with operational reality.

minimumEvidence.artifact: A challenge specification listing obligations on receipt and enumerated outcomes.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A challenge that did not prevail but still produced a recorded reconsideration.
minimumEvidence.metric: Share of challenges producing a recorded state transition of any kind.

entries.title: Consent Depth
entries.bodyHtml:
The distinction between consenting to enter a dependency and consenting to every degree of dependency its operation produces. Adoption is one choice, made once, under one set of alternatives; depth is what accumulates afterwards without any further choice being offered.

The choice at adoption helps manufacture the constrained choice set later. Data accumulates, collaborators organise around the system, alternatives disappear, and the adopter's own competence atrophies, so “you chose this” stops describing the present relationship. Enumerating affected parties at adoption does not close the set either, because people become exposed later without ever having been asked. Bound by STD-02 §10.1 and §10.2.

It matters because standing is usually rationed by original consent. Depth is why corrective standing has to reach anyone who became an error-bearing party after adoption, and why a deepened dependency is where exit coercion operates with nobody applying pressure, leaving a right of exit that is formally intact and practically spent.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
operationalTests: The affected-party set is re-opened at each review rather than fixed at adoption.
Adverse movement in exposure score, substitution cost, or reversibility level since consent is disclosed to the consenting party.
The operator can name the last material deepening of the dependency and show what was disclosed at the time.
entries.genealogy: Separates the Law VII question of who holds standing from the moment of adoption, so consent cannot be used to price a relationship it no longer describes.

minimumEvidence.artifact: A consent record paired with a dated dependency trend showing exposure score, substitution cost, and reversibility level at consent and now.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A disclosure sent to consenting parties when the dependency deepened materially, ahead of the next renewal.
minimumEvidence.metric: Share of material deepenings disclosed within a stated interval, and share of parties who became affected after adoption who hold standing.

entries.title: Constitutional Governance
entries.bodyHtml:
A governance discipline centered on authority grants, jurisdictional boundaries, error-bearing standing, and enforceable recourse, contrasted with behavioral alignment. While alignment asks whether an automated system intends what its creators intend, constitutional governance asks what authority the system holds, what happens when it is wrong or incomplete, and who has the standing to compel correction.

Constitutional governance recognizes that authority cannot be sustained by the absence of observed failure, that evidence and authority must remain coupled, and that the politics of any system are revealed by the rights it grants at the point of model failure.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
operationalTests: Authority is bounded in an explicit grant object with expiration dates and invalidation conditions rather than open-ended permissions.
Error-bearing parties hold procedural standing to initiate review and compel state transitions when systems fail.
entries.genealogy: Distinguishes architectural authority control from behavioral alignment in autonomous and delegated systems.

entries.title: Corrigibility Rent
entries.bodyHtml:
Power gained because others cannot cheaply make you answer for being wrong. A conventional rent comes from holding a scarce position; a corrigibility rent comes from holding a position whose wrongness is expensive to establish — through impossible complaint procedures, proprietary evidence, inaccessible records, inscrutable systems, monopoly expertise, catastrophic exit costs, or appeals that arrive only after the harm has become irreversible.

It matters because it names the portion of authority the framework systematically erodes: not power as such, but the part that survives only because contradiction has been made costly, ineffectual, or invisible. The presumption it reverses is the audit's center of gravity: an institution that wants consequential authority must build and maintain the conditions under which its own wrongness can be established and remedied.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
operationalTests: The cost a challenger bears to establish the institution was wrong is measured and compared with the institution's stake in the outcome.
Records that would establish wrongness are held by the party whose wrongness they would establish.
The meta-question — who decides what happens after someone says no — has a named, answerable owner.
entries.genealogy: Names the rent the casebook's failures were collecting: Robodebt, Horizon, and the childcare-benefits scandal all priced their wrongness beyond their challengers' reach.

minimumEvidence.artifact: A contestation-cost inventory: what a challenger must spend, in time, evidence, and money, to establish an error.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A wrongness-establishing route exercised by a challenge and producing a remedy within the challenger's budget.
minimumEvidence.metric: Share of consequential decisions whose error can be established by the error-bearing party at proportionate cost.

entries.title: Insulation
entries.bodyHtml:
Whatever prevents the consequences of institutional decisions from traveling back to the actors who can revise the generating rules. It can be material (someone else pays), organizational (frontline workers absorb failures before they reach leadership), epistemic (the institution measures completed outcomes but not the labor required to achieve them), procedural (appeals exist but require extraordinary time, persistence, expertise, or money), temporal (consequences arrive after the decision-maker has moved on), social (those who govern rarely encounter those who absorb), legal (responsibility is fragmented or unenforceable), statistical (harm is dispersed so no single event appears consequential), or adaptive (the affected population becomes so skilled at compensating that failure never becomes legible).

Insulation is therefore not merely distance from suffering; it is distance from corrective consequence. The critical structure is cost displacement plus weak feedback plus preserved authority: the more insulated one side is from mismatch, the more adaptive the other side must become, and the more successfully the weaker side adapts, the more insulated the stronger side may become. That self-ratifying loop — bad fit, human adaptation, apparent success, institutional validation, expanded authority — is the workaround presumption run as a governance mechanism.

Not all insulation is bad. Judges may need insulation from immediate political pressure, scientists from popularity, civil servants from retaliation, and minorities from majorities. The distinction is not between insulation and exposure but between insulation from improper pressure and insulation from evidence, accountability, and consequence. The design question is which is being preserved.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
operationalTests: For each decision class, name what travels back when the institution is wrong and the channel it travels through.
Absorbed failures are counted as correction events rather than as successful operations.
Insulation from pressure and insulation from consequence are distinguished, and only the first is preserved.
entries.genealogy: The unifying adversary named in the theory essay on insulation: the closed circuit in which costs are displaced, feedback is weak, and authority is preserved.

minimumEvidence.artifact: A feedback map per decision class: who absorbs the mismatch, what reaches the rule-maker, and what is filtered.
minimumEvidence.behavior: An absorbed failure that reached the rule-maker and produced a rule or category change.
minimumEvidence.metric: Share of consequential decision classes where an absorbed failure reached the rule-maker within a stated clock.

entries.title: Consequential Contradiction
entries.bodyHtml:
The capacity of the world a system governs to force it to reconsider — not merely to complain. Contradiction is consequential when the party bearing the mismatch can make it travel: into the record, the rule, the category, or the jurisdiction that produced it. Domination, in this frame, is power insulated from consequential contradiction: the institution defines the relevant reality, acts on its definition, pushes the residual burden downward, controls what counts as evidence against itself, and cannot be forced to revise by those it gets wrong.

It matters because procedural openness is not the test. A system can receive every complaint and learn nothing — the exception absorption mechanism — and an arrangement can be democratic, public, or participatory and still closed. The test is whether contradiction has state-changing force, which is what the corrective standing register and Law XII's preservation duties exist to secure.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
operationalTests: Contradiction from an affected party can change a rule, category, or authority object, not only their own case.
Disagreement is not auto-classified as user error, anomalous input, or noise without a route that can overturn that classification.
The institution can name the last external contradiction that changed its categories.
entries.genealogy: States the positive form of the domination definition: power is legitimate to the extent it remains exposed to being wrong.

minimumEvidence.artifact: A revision record naming the external contradiction that produced each category or rule change.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A challenge that changes an upstream object rather than only the challenger's outcome.
minimumEvidence.metric: Share of rule or category changes traceable to external contradiction rather than internal review.

entries.title: Halt Stratification
entries.bodyHtml:
Halt authority tiered by blast radius: a frontline operator pausing one case, a supervisor halting a queue, and a steward stopping a system are different instruments with different restoration paths, notification duties, and evidence demands. Stratification is what keeps per-case procedural force from becoming system-wide friction.

It matters because veto-point proliferation — the standing objection to contestability — is what happens when every party holds the same maximal instrument and no one holds a graduated one. Tiering does not remove halt points; it prices them: the power to stop scales with the size of what is being stopped, and the smallest tiers stay cheap enough that people use them.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
operationalTests: Each halt tier names who can fire it, what it stops, and the restoration path at that tier.
A tier-1 halt can be used without escalating to a tier-3 authority.
Restoration capacity is provisioned at each tier, not only at the top.
entries.genealogy: The graduated answer to the vetocracy objection: the theory essay on challenge density argues for pricing halt points by blast radius rather than removing them.

minimumEvidence.artifact: A halt tier register: tiers, authorized roles, blast radius, restoration path, and notification duty per tier.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A halt used at a low tier that resolves without escalation to a higher tier.
minimumEvidence.metric: Share of halts resolved at the tier where they originated.

entries.title: Admission Gate
entries.bodyHtml:
The authorization decision that precedes any grant: whether the system should act at all. An admission gate records the evidence reviewed, the scope considered, and the outcome — including deliberate non-use, which is a decision with reasons and a date, not an absence. A system refused admission has not failed; the refusal is the gate working.

It matters because capability without authority is Law I's object, but the law has a step before the grant that is easy to skip: the evaluation of whether the delegation should exist. Skipping the gate converts a governance question into a momentum question, where the system runs because someone built it and stopping now is more expensive than starting was.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
operationalTests: A consequential deployment has a recorded admission decision with evidence and a named decider.
Deliberate non-use is a recorded outcome with reasons, revisitable on a clock.
"Not yet" and "never" are distinguishable in the record, with different review conditions.
entries.genealogy: Operationalizes Law I at its earliest moment: capability is discovered and catalogued, authority is granted — and the grant decision itself can be no.

minimumEvidence.artifact: An admission decision record: evidence reviewed, scope considered, outcome, and reasons.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A deployment refused admission with the refusal basis recorded and a review condition named.
minimumEvidence.metric: Share of consequential deployments with a recorded admission decision.

entries.title: Dependence Reciprocity
entries.bodyHtml:
Dependence runs both ways. A population that has come to rely on an institution's system has generated duties the institution owes it: notice when the dependency deepens, preservation of exit and alternatives, and continuity obligations at withdrawal. Treating a population's reliance as licence to direct it is a conversion — a fact about dependence turned into an unauthorized permission — and reciprocity is the refusal of that conversion.

It matters because the dependency ledger as usually written records what the institution needs in order to withdraw, and stops there. Reciprocity completes the picture: the crumple zone is not only absorbing cost, it is holding reliance the institution benefits from, and reliance held is a claim, not a resource.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
operationalTests: Dependents are told when their reliance on the system deepens materially.
Withdrawal from a depended-on system carries continuity obligations with dates and owners.
A dependents' claim on the system is recorded with the same standing as the institution's claim on them.
entries.genealogy: Completes Law V: dependence converts technical risk into structural risk, and the conversion runs in the direction of the dependent as well as the institution.

minimumEvidence.artifact: A reciprocity register: dependents, what their reliance holds, and the duties owed at withdrawal.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A material deepening of dependency disclosed to dependents before it takes effect.
minimumEvidence.metric: Share of dependency changes with dependents notified before the change.

entries.title: Corrective Power
entries.bodyHtml:
The effective capacity of affected people to make an arrangement change when its demands become unreasonable: to force reconsideration, reversal, or rule revision, not merely to complain. It is the exercised form of corrective standing — standing names the right, corrective power names whether exercising it can alter the system's governing state.

It matters because it is the second term in the discipline's evaluation formula, alongside outcome and burden: what an arrangement accomplishes, what accomplishing it requires from people, and what power those people hold over those requirements. A system whose corrections are nominal scores high on the first term and low on the third, which what outcomes hide argues is exactly the failure a pure outcome orientation cannot see.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
operationalTests: Affected people can produce a state transition in the arrangement, not only a recorded complaint.
The cost of exercising correction is measured against the capacity of those who must bear it.
Corrective power survives the dependence that justified it being engineered away.
entries.genealogy: Completes the evaluation formula of the outcomes critique: standing made measurable as force rather than as a register entry.

entries.title: Contestability as the Legitimacy Hinge
entries.bodyHtml: A system is legitimate insofar as affected parties have standing, voice, and remedy against its decisions and actions. Contestability is the hinge on which legitimacy turns; legitimacy engineering is the attempt to substitute its appearance for its substance.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
operationalTests: A legitimacy claim is traceable to a standing mechanism, not to messaging.
Loss of remedy is scored as loss of legitimacy, not as an operational detail.
entries.genealogy: States the democratic premise that ties legitimacy to enforceable remedy.

entries.title: Maintenance Budgets are Legitimacy Budgets
entries.bodyHtml:
The capacity to monitor, review, and repair is a political and organizational legitimacy input, not overhead. An institution that cannot afford maintenance is running down a debt it will collect as illegitimacy.

Unfunded repair is unfunded legitimacy.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
operationalTests: Review and repair capacity is budgeted alongside feature work.
A maintenance cut is evaluated as a legitimacy cut, not a cost saving.
entries.genealogy: Reclassifies upkeep from operational expense to the currency of legitimacy.

entries.title: Receipts-by-Default as a Legitimacy Interface
entries.bodyHtml:
People should automatically get “what happened” records: actions taken, permissions used, reasons, and accountable owners. A liability record or attestation is not a favor; it is the default output of an accountable act.

Receipts make recordkeeping symmetric instead of a lever held only by the institution.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
operationalTests: Every consequential action produces a receipt without being requested.
A receipt names an accountable owner and a clock for the next step.
entries.genealogy: Elevates receipts from a transparency nicety to a governance default.

entries.title: Sovereignty as Constraint-Imposition Capacity
entries.bodyHtml: Sovereignty is the ability to impose enforceable constraints on infrastructure operating in your territory. Without it, design authority belongs to whoever owns the stack, and path dependence locks in their defaults.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
operationalTests: A jurisdiction can bind foreign infrastructure to local remedy and audit rules.
Constraint-imposition capacity is measured, not assumed from legal text.
entries.genealogy: Reframes sovereignty as an engineering capacity, not a legal claim.

entries.title: Standards Wars as Recourse Wars
entries.bodyHtml: Global competition shifts to whose regimes for auditability, liability, and redress become default through supply chains and procurement. The war is not over features but over whose restitution and governability rules travel with the product.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
operationalTests: Procurement criteria weight redress and auditability, not only performance.
A standard is judged by the remedy it binds, not the language it adopts.
entries.genealogy: Reads international standards competition as competition over enforceable recourse.

entries.title: Democratic vs Coercive Governability
entries.bodyHtml: Governance infrastructure can either enable rights-preserving contestability or scaled conduct control, depending on who has standing and remedy. Governability is neutral; its direction is set by whether standing is distributed or concentrated.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
operationalTests: The distribution of standing is stated and measurable.
A governability claim specifies whose remedy it protects.
entries.genealogy: Splits governability along the axis that determines whether it serves or coerces.

entries.title: Bindingness
entries.bodyHtml:
The degree to which a system’s outputs create enforceable obligations—deadlines, duties, remedies, or reversals—rather than mere communications. Bindingness is the difference between “we received your request” and “we must decide by Friday or you win.”

It is the property that bindingness after contact describes at the moment of interaction, and that binding clocks make time-bound.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
operationalTests: An output is classified as binding or non-binding on its face.
A binding output names the obligation it creates and the authority that enforces it.
entries.genealogy: Makes enforceability the defining property of an institutional utterance.

entries.title: Non-bindingness / Nonbindingness
entries.bodyHtml:
The condition where a system can interact, respond, and even apologize without being compelled to change state. Non-bindingness is power without accountability: activity without obligation.

It is the substrate on which delay as power and unearned closure operate, and the opposite of bindingness.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
operationalTests: A response is scored by whether it can change state, not by how helpful it sounds.
Activity that cannot bind is flagged as non-binding rather than counted as remedy.
entries.genealogy: Names the default posture of institutions that prefer communication to correction.

entries.title: Standing (vs Belief)
entries.bodyHtml:
Standing is the recognized right to make the system bind itself to engage, decide, and remedy—regardless of whether your story is believed, liked, or emotionally legible. “Belief” is narrative validation; standing is enforceable access to decision power.

Corrective standing is the test: can this person force a correction, or only be heard?
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
operationalTests: Access to remedy does not depend on being believed or found sympathetic.
Standing is granted by rule and survives disagreement over the claimant’s narrative.
entries.genealogy: Separates enforceable access from narrative validation, the core distinction of the remedy vocabulary.

entries.title: Binding Authority
entries.bodyHtml:
A person or role that can change the underlying state and is obligated to respond. Binding authority is not “a human is involved”; it is a human with power + duty + traceable accountability.

It is what distinguishes real review from a human-in-the-loop legitimacy artifact, and what decision reversal authority requires.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
operationalTests: Every review stage names a role that can change state, not merely comment.
The accountable owner is traceable from the decision to the record.
entries.genealogy: Defines the authority threshold that separates remedy from review theater.

entries.title: Evidence Parity
entries.bodyHtml:
A condition where affected people have a fair chance to meet the evidentiary burden—access to the relevant facts, rules, and records—rather than being asked to prove things the institution can’t or won’t disclose. Without evidence parity, appeals become theater.

It is the answer to evidence burden ceilings and evidence recycling.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
operationalTests: The institution discloses the facts it used, before the claimant must respond.
An evidentiary burden is matched to what the claimant could reasonably access.
entries.genealogy: Makes fairness a property of access to evidence, not of procedure alone.

entries.title: Authority Chain
entries.bodyHtml: The mapping of who can change what state, at which stage, under what constraints. Authority chains determine whether escalation is real. They are built from authority grants and leases along a delegation chain.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
operationalTests: Every state change traces to a named authority at a named stage.
A broken authority chain (a stage with no one able to change state) is a defect.
entries.genealogy: Renders the structure of escalation explicit so it can be audited.

entries.title: Authority Mutation
entries.bodyHtml:
A pattern where escalation changes how the institution speaks without changing who has power to reverse outcomes. Authority mutates when the channel upgrades (more polite, more official, more complex) but the underlying ability to bind remains absent.

It is the specific failure of escalation reliability, and the cousin of authority drift.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
operationalTests: Escalation is scored by change in binding power, not change in tone or channel.
A channel upgrade without a power upgrade is flagged as mutation, not progress.
entries.genealogy: Names the substitution of surface escalation for real escalation.

entries.title: Defaults (as Governance)
entries.bodyHtml:
The idea that the baseline state—what happens if nobody intervenes—is a primary allocator of outcomes and costs. Defaults govern by deciding who must spend time, attention, and stamina to avoid harm.

They are the silent partner of auto-close, auto-renew, auto-share, and the enemy of meaningful control.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
operationalTests: Every default is audited for who bears the cost of escaping it.
A default is chosen by the party who would bear its harm, not only its benefit.
entries.genealogy: Elevates the default from a UX detail to a governance instrument.

entries.title: Procedural Caste
entries.bodyHtml:
A stratification system where people are divided by their ability to force binding action: who can start clocks, reach authorities, obtain reversals, and make claims legible. It is a caste system of enforceability, not worth.

It is produced by procedural burden priced as access and sustained by access cliffs and stamina pricing.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
operationalTests: Enforceability is measured as a distribution across people, not a binary.
A procedural barrier is audited for who it sorts out of remedy.
entries.genealogy: Recasts procedural friction as a mechanism of social stratification.

entries.title: Escalation (without Authority)
entries.bodyHtml:
A channel change that does not increase binding power—more forms, more tiers, more waiting—while the underlying decision remains unchangeable. It is escalation as delay management, not remedy.

It is the lived form of authority mutation and a vehicle for delay as power.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
operationalTests: Escalation that cannot reach a decision-reversal authority is not counted as recourse.
Tier counts are not confused with binding-power counts.
entries.genealogy: Distinguishes moving up a channel from moving toward a binding decision.

entries.title: Redress
entries.bodyHtml:
The set of mechanisms that can correct harm: appeal, review, reversal, compensation, restoration. Redress is real when it is time-bound and reaches binding authority.

It is the umbrella over the restitution ladder, remedy equivalence, and decision reversal authority.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
operationalTests: Every harm type has a mapped redress path with a clock and an owner.
A redress path is tested end-to-end, not described in policy.
entries.genealogy: Unifies the correction mechanisms under a single time-bound standard.

entries.title: Override Path
entries.bodyHtml:
A defined mechanism that can supersede the default workflow when the default would cause harm: human escalation with real authority, emergency reversal, or exception handling with deadlines. Override paths are where a stated commitment to people becomes a mechanism.

They are the practical form of intervention specification and the release valve on safe pause.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
