operationalTests: Every default workflow has a named override with a deadline.
An override changes the underlying state; a changed conversation alone does not count.
entries.genealogy: Converts good intentions into a defined, enforceable escape hatch.

entries.title: Structured Exit
entries.bodyHtml:
An exit process designed to protect the leaver: clear steps, data portability, timelines, anti-retaliation constraints, and closure that doesn’t require ongoing performance. Structured exit turns leaving into a governed pathway instead of an endurance test.

It is the machinery behind the right of exit, and the answer to exit cost and exit coercion.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
operationalTests: Leaving has bounded steps, a deadline, and portability, not open-ended performance.
Exit carries a non-retaliation guarantee rather than reputational risk.
entries.genealogy: Makes exit a governed right rather than a test of endurance.

entries.title: Paywalled Rights
entries.bodyHtml:
When access to contestation, speed, or binding review is effectively purchased—through fees, premium support, lawyers, consultants, or time flexibility. Rights exist, but only for those who can pay in money or stamina.

It is the price form of the access cliff and of stamina pricing.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
operationalTests: Access to remedy is not gated by payment or discretionary free time.
A right that requires a professional intermediary to exercise is flagged as paywalled.
entries.genealogy: Exposes the economic gate that turns formal rights into practical privileges.

entries.title: Logs-as-power
entries.bodyHtml:
The idea that control over records—what is logged, who can see it, what counts as evidence—shapes who can contest outcomes. Recordkeeping is governance.

It is why attestation and the liability record matter, and why evidence parity is a rights question.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
operationalTests: The evidentiary record is accessible to the affected party by default.
What is (and is not) logged is itself an accountable design decision.
entries.genealogy: Makes the log a site of power rather than a technical afterthought.

entries.title: Audit Trail
entries.bodyHtml:
A trace of events and decisions—what happened, when, by whom, under what rule—used for accountability. Audit trails matter only if they connect to reversal power.

They are the raw material of the liability record and the policy record, and feed traceable ownership.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
operationalTests: Every consequential state change leaves a trace naming owner, rule, and time.
The trail reaches a decision-reversal authority rather than dead-ending in a log.
entries.genealogy: Binds recordkeeping to its purpose: making correction possible.

entries.title: Administrative Reality
entries.bodyHtml:
The world as the system recognizes it: what counts, what is recordable, what triggers action. Administrative reality often diverges from lived reality.

It is the boundary drawn by legibility, the gate that harm receipts must cross, and the field in which object formation either succeeds or fails.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
operationalTests: A lived harm can be tested for whether it exists in the administrative record.
The divergence between lived and administrative reality is measured, not denied.
entries.genealogy: Names the recognition boundary that determines what can be contested.

entries.title: Contract of Adhesion
entries.bodyHtml:
A take-it-or-leave-it contract offered by a more powerful party where negotiation is impossible; a common substrate for coerced “choice.” It is the legal form of coercive consent.

Where adhesion is total, consent depth is zero and refusability is forfeited by signing.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
operationalTests: The power asymmetry behind a contract is measured, not assumed away.
Terms that are unavoidable are audited as defaults, not as negotiated consent.
entries.genealogy: Imports the contract-law concept that underlies much coerced “choice.”

entries.title: NDA Retaliation / Narrative Erasure
entries.bodyHtml:
Mechanisms that suppress exit stories—legal threats, informal retaliation, reputational control—preventing systems from being held accountable by shared evidence. They extend the retaliation surface beyond the employment relationship.

They are what a non-retaliation guarantee must cancel, and a driver of exit coercion.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
operationalTests: Silencing mechanisms are named and countered, not treated as neutral legal practice.
Exit stories can be shared without retaliation, by design and by rule.
entries.genealogy: Connects legal silencing to the erasure of the evidence that remedies require.

entries.title: Decision Threshold
entries.bodyHtml:
The score, cut-off, or confidence floor that decides whether an action runs unattended, goes to a person, or is refused. In a deployment gated by a classifier or a typed decision model, the threshold is where authority is conferred: the model proposes, and the number decides what the institution lets it do.

It matters because thresholds are usually held as configuration, tuned once against one model version and never recorded as a decision. STD-08 §2.6 holds a decision threshold as a policy record whose assumptions name the labelled cases, model version, question schema, and option order it was set against, with a review trigger on any change to them. Where the threshold also chooses what reaches a reviewer, it is part of the intervention specification.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
operationalTests: Every threshold that routes a consequential action resolves to a policy record with provenance, assumptions, review triggers, and an expiry.
The policy record names the model version, question schema, and option order the threshold was tuned against, and the production values match it.
A change to the model version, schema, or option order moves the threshold's policy record to review_required.
entries.genealogy: Gives Law III an object at the point where typed decision models locate authority: the evidence for a threshold is the labelled data and the model version it was set against, and it decays when either changes.

references.label: Typed decision models and where their authority lives

minimumEvidence.artifact: A policy record for each routing threshold, naming its tuning set, pinned model version, schema, and option order.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A model upgrade or option reorder moving the threshold's policy record to review_required before it gates another action.
minimumEvidence.metric: Share of routing thresholds backed by a policy record pinned to the model version in production.

entries.title: Shaping Hop
entries.bodyHtml:
A component that routes, orders, ranks, filters, or drops the cases, inputs, or evidence a consequential decision is made on, without making the decision itself. Triage classifiers, retrieval filters, priority routers, and model routers that pick which delegate decides are all shaping hops.

It matters because each call looks like plumbing, so none is granted, while together they decide whose case waits, which evidence the decider never sees, and which applicant reaches a person. STD-09 §1.5 enumerates shaping hops in the delegation chain and assesses their consequence in aggregate. STD-09 §1.6 treats a hop that selects the delegate at run time as a delegation over its whole range, so every delegate it can choose is granted and each decision record names the one that decided.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
operationalTests: Every component that routes, ranks, filters, or drops a consequential decision's inputs appears in the head grant's chain.
Each shaping hop's consequence is reported in aggregate, such as wait times or evidence excluded, not per call.
Decision records name the delegate a router selected, and the router's full range is enumerated.
entries.genealogy: Extends Law I one boundary further: capability that shapes a decision through a hop nobody granted is capability outrunning authority, however small each output looks.

references.label: Typed decision models and where their authority lives

minimumEvidence.artifact: A chain enumeration that lists every routing, ranking, and filtering component, with the grant each runs under.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A new triage classifier or router candidate recorded as a chain event before it runs.
minimumEvidence.metric: Share of decision records that name every hop that shaped them, including the delegate a router selected.

entries.title: Confidence-Gated Execution
entries.bodyHtml:
An arrangement in which a model's confidence decides whether an action runs unattended, goes to a person, or is refused. It is sold as oversight that scales: high-confidence cases run, and people see only the uncertain ones.

It matters because it moves both authority and review into a number. The threshold confers the authority, so STD-08 §2.6 holds it as a decision threshold policy. The threshold also chooses the reviewer's queue, so STD-08 §3.6 makes it part of the intervention specification and sends a sample of the confident cases to review too, because a queue fed only with uncertain cases cannot detect a confident error. Without both, the arrangement is human oversight in name only.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
operationalTests: The routing threshold resolves to a pinned policy record and is named on the intervention specification.
A declared share of decisions that ran unattended reaches review, and its reversal rate is reported apart from the routed queue.
The record states whether the reviewer sees the model's score.
entries.genealogy: Applies Law IX to review queues selected by a score: a person who only ever sees the cases the model was unsure of cannot alter what the model was sure of.

minimumEvidence.artifact: An intervention specification with a routing block naming the threshold policy, whether the score is shown, and the unreviewed sample.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A threshold change opening a reconsideration of the intervention specification.
minimumEvidence.metric: Reversal rate in the sample of decisions that ran unattended, reported apart from the routed queue.

entries.title: Systemic Refusal
entries.bodyHtml:
Systemic refusal is the deliberate collective refusal by human operators, caseworkers, or subjects to absorb automated system failures or perform uncounted compensatory labor, returning the true cost of unviable system operations to the institution in real time.

Refusing to absorb systemic shock is not obstruction; it is the only form of structural honesty that compels an institution to register and repair defects in automated decision systems.
examples: Claims examiners decline to fix garbled automated decision notices by hand, routing them back to the automated pipeline and surfacing the defect to executive leadership.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
operationalTests: Operators adhere strictly to documented procedures and standard working hours, routing all unhandled edge cases to formal escalation queues.
Systemic refusal produces immediate operational signal that compels management to address root design defects rather than patching symptoms.
entries.genealogy: Derived from labor work-to-rule practices and andon cord manufacturing protocols, transforming private exhaustion into public accountability.

categories.heading: I. Friction & flow
categories.descriptionHtml: Where a system slows, pauses, or asks for confirmation before it acts, and who carries the cost of that friction.

entries.title: Protective Friction
entries.bodyHtml:
Friction intentionally added to slow harmful processes and keep moral latency within safe bounds. Protective friction inserts checkpoints where speed would otherwise amplify risk.

It should be targeted and proportional: enough to prevent harm, not enough to create punitive burden.
entries.scope: I. Friction & flow. Where a system slows, pauses, or asks for confirmation before it acts, and who carries the cost of that friction.
examples: High-risk account changes require a second authenticated confirmation before execution.

entries.title: Punitive Friction
entries.bodyHtml:
Friction that punishes users through unnecessary loops, opaque requirements, or repeated proof demands. Punitive friction often masks extraction by endurance as policy.

Unlike protective friction, it raises cost without improving safety or repair outcomes.
entries.scope: I. Friction & flow. Where a system slows, pauses, or asks for confirmation before it acts, and who carries the cost of that friction.
examples: A dispute process forces users through multiple redundant forms before any human review is allowed.

entries.title: Procedural Burden as Price
entries.bodyHtml:
Paperwork and “friction” are not incidental; they are rationing mechanisms that should be capped, disclosed, or penalized.

Procedural burden as price exposes punitive friction and steepens the burden gradient.
entries.scope: I. Friction & flow. Where a system slows, pauses, or asks for confirmation before it acts, and who carries the cost of that friction.

entries.title: Dignity Friction
entries.bodyHtml:
Friction that preserves autonomy, such as double checks on irreversible actions and plain-language confirmation states. Dignity friction helps people understand consequences before commitment without shaming them for caution.

It differs from punitive friction because the cost is proportional to risk and paired with clear pathways forward.
examples: Before account deletion, the interface requires a brief confirmation with restore options and support contact details.
entries.scope: I. Friction & flow. Where a system slows, pauses, or asks for confirmation before it acts, and who carries the cost of that friction.

entries.title: Velocity Friction
entries.bodyHtml:
Friction added specifically to prevent runaway system behaviors in high-speed workflows. Velocity friction creates deliberate pauses before scale multiplies harm.

Common mechanisms include rate limits, staged rollouts, and mandatory human checkpoints tied to ethical interrupts.
entries.scope: I. Friction & flow. Where a system slows, pauses, or asks for confirmation before it acts, and who carries the cost of that friction.
examples: A recommendation engine rollout is throttled by cohort with auto-pause triggers when harmful engagement signals rise.

entries.title: Safety Valve
entries.bodyHtml:
A deliberate release point that lets people slow, pause, or reroute automation before harm compounds.

Safety valves pair stoppability with dignity friction so flows with serious consequences default to reversible states and route to humans without penalty.
entries.scope: I. Friction & flow. Where a system slows, pauses, or asks for confirmation before it acts, and who carries the cost of that friction.

entries.title: Consent Journey
entries.bodyHtml:
The sequenced touchpoints where a person learns what a system will do, grants or denies permission, and can revise that choice over time.

Strong consent journeys use anticipatory consent, visible permission surfaces, and healthy refusal budgets so pausing or exiting does not jeopardize access or service.

A journey that ends at adoption misses consent depth: the dependency keeps deepening after the permission was granted, and the choice has to be reopened rather than remembered.
entries.scope: I. Friction & flow. Where a system slows, pauses, or asks for confirmation before it acts, and who carries the cost of that friction.

entries.title: Humane Friction
entries.bodyHtml:
The combination of protective, dignity, and velocity friction across a whole workflow, placed so the process slows only where risk, irreversibility, or coercion pressure is high.

Each point of friction can be explained, removed, and measured, and it reduces later harm without trapping people in needless process.
examples: A lending flow adds extra verification only for high-risk decisions and offers an accessible appeal path when checks block approval.
entries.scope: I. Friction & flow. Where a system slows, pauses, or asks for confirmation before it acts, and who carries the cost of that friction.

entries.title: Appropriate Friction
entries.bodyHtml: Deliberate slowdowns or checkpoints inserted where harm would be costly or irreversible. Appropriate friction treats velocity friction and ethical interrupts as safety features.
examples: High-risk data exports require a second reviewer before completion.
entries.scope: I. Friction & flow. Where a system slows, pauses, or asks for confirmation before it acts, and who carries the cost of that friction.

entries.title: Frictionless Harm
entries.bodyHtml: Harms that spread unchecked because safeguards or pauses were stripped away. Frictionless harm is the inverse of protective friction; it appears when velocity friction and dignity friction are absent.
entries.scope: I. Friction & flow. Where a system slows, pauses, or asks for confirmation before it acts, and who carries the cost of that friction.

entries.title: Coercive Consent
entries.bodyHtml:
“Agreement” obtained through defaults, asymmetry, or threats of exclusion—consent produced by lack of viable refusal. It is the opposite of consent depth.

It is manufactured by contracts of adhesion and refusability failures, and laundered by dropout-as-legitimation.
entries.scope: I. Friction & flow. Where a system slows, pauses, or asks for confirmation before it acts, and who carries the cost of that friction.
operationalTests: Consent is scored by the viability of refusal, not the presence of an “I agree” click.
A default that excludes on refusal is flagged as coercive regardless of wording.
entries.genealogy: Defines consent by the real option to refuse, not by the signature.

categories.heading: J. Decision states & edges
categories.descriptionHtml: Where and how decisions flip from reversible to permanent.

entries.title: Decision Edge
entries.bodyHtml: The precise moment when a choice shifts from reversible to consequential. Making the decision edge visible enables dignity friction, clearer consent, and routing to ethical interrupts when risk spikes.
entries.scope: J. Decision states & edges. Where and how decisions flip from reversible to permanent.

entries.title: Decision Artifact
entries.bodyHtml:
A discrete, attributable, contestable output: outcome + reason + timestamp + accountable owner.

Decision artifacts anchor traceable ownership and make contestability measurable.

Minimum evidence

  • User-facing artifact.
  • Internal log.
  • Drill / rehearsal.
entries.scope: J. Decision states & edges. Where and how decisions flip from reversible to permanent.

entries.title: Decision Object
entries.bodyHtml:
Normative definition. A Decision Object is a versioned, inspectable record that encodes the rules, inputs, thresholds, and authority governing an operational decision.

A decision object is a governance artifact in its own right, not only a piece of logic. They must specify ownership, appealability, reversibility, and temporal obligations. Decisions that affect access, status, or rights must be backed by an active decision object.

Minimal JSON schema (governance-grade).

{
  "decision_object_id": "DO-ACCESS-0041",
  "decision_name": "Eligibility Determination",
  "status": "active",
  "owner_role": "Risk Operations",
  "authority": {
    "issuing_body": "Eligibility Committee",
    "delegation_basis": "Policy §4.2"
  },
  "inputs": [
    {"name": "income_verified", "type": "boolean"},
    {"name": "employment_duration_months", "type": "integer"}
  ],
  "decision_logic": {
    "model_type": "ruleset",
    "description": "Income verification + minimum employment duration"
  },
  "outputs": [
    {"value": "approved"},
    {"value": "denied"},
    {"value": "pending_review"}
  ],
  "reversibility": {
    "allowed": true,
    "mechanism": "human_override",
    "reversal_sla_id": "RSLA-002"
  },
  "contestability": {
    "appealable": true,
    "appeal_channel": "formal_request",
    "binding_clock_id": "BC-010"
  },
  "audit": {
    "last_updated": "2026-01-10",
    "version": "1.3.0",
    "change_log_ref": "CH-884"
  }
}

Ethotechnics move. This reframes “the system decided” into “this object did.” Once the object exists, accountability stops being philosophical.
entries.scope: J. Decision states & edges. Where and how decisions flip from reversible to permanent.

entries.title: Binding Clock
entries.bodyHtml:
Normative definition. A Binding Clock is an enforceable timer governing system obligations once a decision enters a pending or contested state.

The clock continues to accrue regardless of internal workload, staffing constraints, or review queues unless explicitly paused under defined conditions.

Clock semantics (design-legible).

binding_clock_id: BC-010
trigger_event: decision_status == "pending_review"
start_condition: timestamp_of_trigger
pause_conditions:
  - mutual_extension_agreed
  - documented_external_dependency
pause_requires:
  approver_role: Ombuds Officer
  public_log: true
timeout_effects:
  - default_to_human_review
  - interim_access_granted
clock_visibility: user_visible

Why this matters. Without a binding clock, delay is power, silence is treated as consent, and “we’re reviewing” becomes infinite. With it, time itself becomes a governed surface and institutions pay for waiting.
entries.scope: J. Decision states & edges. Where and how decisions flip from reversible to permanent.

entries.title: Reversal SLA
entries.bodyHtml:
Normative definition. A Reversal SLA specifies maximum allowable time, authority, and procedure for undoing or correcting a decision once contested or found erroneous.

Reversal performance is a core reliability metric, not an exception.

Contract-ready clause.

Reversal Commitment. Upon receipt of a valid reversal request, Provider shall initiate human review within 24 hours and complete reversal or affirm decision within 5 business days. Failure to meet this obligation shall result in interim restoration of access and applicable service credits.

Operational metrics (what you track).

{
  "reversal_sla_id": "RSLA-002",
  "time_to_human_hours": 24,
  "time_to_reversal_days": 5,
  "escalation_path": [
    "Ops Lead",
    "Risk Director",
    "Independent Reviewer"
  ],
  "breach_consequence": "automatic_interim_restoration"
}

Ethotechnics move. Most systems optimize time-to-deny. This forces optimization of time-to-repair.

Interlock. Decision Objects define what happened and who owns it. Binding Clocks govern how long uncertainty is allowed to exist. Reversal SLAs enforce how quickly harm must be undone. Together, “You can appeal” becomes “Appeal changes the system’s obligations.”

entries.title: Non-Decision
entries.bodyHtml:
A stable administrative disposition where a system withholds a contestable outcome (“pending,” “in review”) while consequences accrue.

Non-decisions stretch moral latency and erode contestability by keeping people in limbo.
entries.scope: J. Decision states & edges. Where and how decisions flip from reversible to permanent.

entries.title: Unearned Closure
entries.bodyHtml:
The system marks something resolved without repairing the underlying harm; the residual cost remains with the person.

Unearned closure converts unresolved obligations into status changes and often hides behind attrition-as-resolution or closure-code regimes.
entries.scope: J. Decision states & edges. Where and how decisions flip from reversible to permanent.

entries.title: Stable Clock
entries.bodyHtml:
A non-resettable timeline for a case; the system cannot restart time via re-ticketing, re-verification, or channel switching.

Stable clocks enforce bounded duration and keep timelines legible.
entries.scope: J. Decision states & edges. Where and how decisions flip from reversible to permanent.

entries.title: Utility Window
entries.bodyHtml:
The time span during which relief can still prevent the relevant harm.

Designing for a clear utility window keeps time-to-restore accountable.
entries.scope: J. Decision states & edges. Where and how decisions flip from reversible to permanent.

entries.title: Utility Expiry
entries.bodyHtml:
Crossing the utility window; relief arrives too late to matter.

Utility expiry converts support into paperwork and should trigger constructive denial or repair.
entries.scope: J. Decision states & edges. Where and how decisions flip from reversible to permanent.

entries.title: Futility Threshold
entries.bodyHtml:
The point where time-on-task or repetition becomes so costly that valid claimants predictably abandon pursuit.

Systems that hit the futility threshold signal punitive friction and low contestability.
entries.scope: J. Decision states & edges. Where and how decisions flip from reversible to permanent.

entries.title: Constructive Denial
entries.bodyHtml:
A legal state where delay is treated as refusal because it destroys utility or makes pursuit futile.

Constructive denial recognizes utility expiry and forces accountable remedies.
entries.scope: J. Decision states & edges. Where and how decisions flip from reversible to permanent.

entries.title: Critical Action
entries.bodyHtml: Any system action that meaningfully alters a person’s status, access, or trajectory. Critical actions require dignity friction.
entries.scope: J. Decision states & edges. Where and how decisions flip from reversible to permanent.

entries.title: Irreversible Boundary
entries.bodyHtml: A threshold the system cannot automatically undo—account closures, public releases, or data publication. Crossing it demands heightened contestability, audited explanations, and explicit time-to-restore plans.
entries.scope: J. Decision states & edges. Where and how decisions flip from reversible to permanent.

entries.title: Ethical Interrupts
entries.bodyHtml:
Automatic system-level halts triggered by anomalies, harm indicators, or policy boundary breaches. Ethical interrupts operationalize stoppability by turning warning signals into enforceable pauses.

They must include clear ownership, audit trails, and restart criteria so pauses protect people without becoming arbitrary lockouts.
entries.scope: J. Decision states & edges. Where and how decisions flip from reversible to permanent.
examples: A model-serving pipeline halts promotion when subgroup harm metrics breach policy limits and requires cross-functional signoff before restart.

entries.title: Actionability Threshold
entries.bodyHtml: The level of confidence, authorization, and oversight required before information becomes action. Raising the actionability threshold protects against low-signal decisions and clarifies design authority.
examples: A fraud alert triggers action only after confidence and authorization checks.
entries.scope: J. Decision states & edges. Where and how decisions flip from reversible to permanent.

entries.title: Normative Uncertainty
entries.bodyHtml: Situations where it is unclear what the “right” action is, requiring caution, clarification, or human judgment rather than confident automation. Normative uncertainty often triggers ethical interrupts and a higher actionability threshold.
examples: When guidance conflicts, the system pauses and requests human judgment.
entries.scope: J. Decision states & edges. Where and how decisions flip from reversible to permanent.

entries.title: Harm Receipt
entries.bodyHtml: A claimant-facing artifact documenting what happened, what the system believes, and what it will do next, by when. Harm receipts make decision artifacts legible to affected people.
entries.scope: J. Decision states & edges. Where and how decisions flip from reversible to permanent.
operationalTests: Receipts are issued automatically for defined incident classes and include named owner and clock.
Receipts capture what happened, the system’s belief, and the next steps with timelines.

entries.title: Access Cliff
entries.bodyHtml: A threshold where small variance causes catastrophic loss of service, such as lockout, termination, or loss of benefits. Access cliffs are mitigated with soft edges and gradual ramps.
entries.scope: J. Decision states & edges. Where and how decisions flip from reversible to permanent.
operationalTests: An access cliff inventory exists with mandated soft edges or gradual ramps.
Policies prohibit catastrophic loss from minor variance without a graduated path.

entries.title: Expansion Decision
entries.bodyHtml:
A separate authorization decision taken when an existing delegation is widened in scope, population, autonomy, or consequence. It carries its own evidence, its own correction capacity check, and its own dependence review, and it is recorded as a transition on the grant.

It matters because expansion is normally treated as the reward for success rather than as a new delegation. Requiring the decision is the direct block on the automation ratchet, and it keeps an authority grant readable against what the system now does.
entries.scope: J. Decision states & edges. Where and how decisions flip from reversible to permanent.
operationalTests: Widening a delegation cannot be shipped without an expansion record naming its evidence.
The record includes a correction capacity check and a dependence review, not only a risk note.
Expansion transitions are visible in the grant's state history.
entries.genealogy: Turns Law XI into a decision state, so that growth in delegated authority has the same ceremony as its creation.

minimumEvidence.artifact: An expansion record with evidence, correction capacity check, and dependence review.
minimumEvidence.behavior: An expansion deferred because correction capacity had not grown with the proposed scope.
minimumEvidence.metric: Share of scope increases accompanied by an expansion record.
minimumEvidence.threshold: Target 100 percent; gaps are reconciled as authority drift.

entries.title: Non-Finality
entries.bodyHtml:
The property that a decisive action does not close its own categories, evidence, or jurisdiction against revision. A system with non-finality can act now and be corrected later; a system whose decisions become final by default converts each exercise of power into an entitlement. Appeal is its instrument at the level of outcomes, and meta-contestability extends it to the rules of challenge themselves.

It matters because finality is how power consolidates quietly: an initial judgment that cannot be reopened becomes precedent for the next, and the category that produced the judgment becomes harder to question than the judgment itself. The rights tradition names the interruption — appeal interrupts the conversion of decision into finality — and Law XII bars consuming the capacity that keeps it possible.
entries.scope: J. Decision states & edges. Where and how decisions flip from reversible to permanent.
operationalTests: A decided outcome can be reopened on stated grounds without extraordinary procedure.
Categories and evidentiary rules stay revisable after decisions were made under them.
The institution's jurisdiction itself can be challenged, not only its outcomes.
entries.genealogy: Completes the framework's five concerns — jurisdiction, representation, residual custody, corrigibility, and the property that keeps all four revisable.

minimumEvidence.artifact: A reopen register: decided outcomes with the grounds and clock on which each can be reopened.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A decision reopened on stated grounds, with the category or rule it questioned still changeable.
minimumEvidence.metric: Share of consequential decision classes with a stated reopen route and clock.

entries.title: Decision Surface
entries.bodyHtml:
The part of a system where decisions become visible, addressable, and contestable. Many systems minimize the decision surface to avoid accountability.

It is the territory shaped by the interaction surface, populated by decision objects, and opened or closed by contestability.
entries.scope: J. Decision states & edges. Where and how decisions flip from reversible to permanent.
operationalTests: Every consequential decision exposes a surface that can be addressed.
A shrinking decision surface is treated as a governance regression.
entries.genealogy: Makes the addressability of decisions a designed, auditable property.

entries.title: Object Formation
entries.bodyHtml:
The process by which a complaint, harm, or request becomes a decision object—assigned an identifier, a category, an owner, a standard of review, and a clock. Systems often block accountability by preventing object formation (“nothing exists to appeal”).

It is the gate that a harm receipt must pass to become a decision object.
entries.scope: J. Decision states & edges. Where and how decisions flip from reversible to permanent.
operationalTests: Every received harm forms an object with id, owner, standard, and clock.
Failure to form an object is an auditable failure, not a filing quirk.
entries.genealogy: Makes the birth of a decision object a governed event rather than an assumption.

entries.title: Pending / Pendingness
entries.bodyHtml:
A default state where nothing is decided and no one is obligated—often presented as neutral but functioning as an outcome allocator. Pendingness becomes harm when it lacks a clock, an owner, or a forced next step.

It is the warm form of non-finality, sustained by delay as power when no binding clock runs.
entries.scope: J. Decision states & edges. Where and how decisions flip from reversible to permanent.
operationalTests: Every pending state carries a clock and an owner by default.
Indefinite pending without obligation is flagged as harm, not neutrality.
entries.genealogy: Reveals the neutral-sounding “pending” as an allocator of outcomes.

entries.title: Settlement
entries.bodyHtml:
The moment a claim becomes resolved in a way that changes the underlying state—approved, denied with appeal rights, remediated, reversed, paid, restored, or otherwise closed with consequences. Settlement is not closure in the CRM; it is resolution that binds.

It is the outcome that bindingness makes possible and that closure-code regimes often fake.
entries.scope: J. Decision states & edges. Where and how decisions flip from reversible to permanent.
operationalTests: A settled claim changes underlying state, not only its ticket status.
Settlement is distinguished from closure that binds nothing.
entries.genealogy: Reserves “settled” for resolution that binds the institution.

entries.title: Non-settlement / Nonsettlement
entries.bodyHtml:
An institutional mode where claims are acknowledged and processed indefinitely without producing a binding resolution. The system offers intake, updates, and politeness while keeping obligation optional.

It is the operational home of attrition as resolution and unearned closure.
entries.scope: J. Decision states & edges. Where and how decisions flip from reversible to permanent.
operationalTests: A claim is scored by whether it reached binding resolution, not by how long it was processed.
Institutions distinguish activity on a claim from settlement of it.
entries.genealogy: Names the indefinite-processing mode that pretends to be adjudication.

entries.title: Clock-start / Clock mismatch
entries.bodyHtml:
Clock-start: the moment a system becomes time-bound—deadlines begin, obligations attach, escalation becomes meaningful. Clock mismatch: when institutional execution is fast (instant flags, freezes, denials) but redress is slow (weeks-months of human review), making errors durable and contestation scarce.

It is the temporal form of binding clocks versus reversal SLAs.
entries.scope: J. Decision states & edges. Where and how decisions flip from reversible to permanent.
operationalTests: Every decision has a defined clock-start, not an open-ended one.
Execution and redress latency are compared; a large gap is flagged as a defect.
entries.genealogy: Makes the asymmetry between action speed and correction speed explicit.

entries.title: Slow Redress / Fast Execution
entries.bodyHtml:
A governance asymmetry where harmful state changes are immediate but appeals are delayed, discretionary, and exhausting. This is one of the main engines of modern coercion.

It is degradation-restoration asymmetry in its temporal form, and what time-to-restore is measured against.
entries.scope: J. Decision states & edges. Where and how decisions flip from reversible to permanent.
operationalTests: Harm and remedy latencies are measured separately and compared.
A fast-execution/slow-redress gap is treated as a coercion indicator, not a cost tradeoff.
entries.genealogy: Isolates the speed asymmetry that makes harm cheap and correction expensive.

entries.title: Irreversibility
entries.bodyHtml:
A state where reversal is practically unavailable (too slow, too expensive, too discretionary) even if it is theoretically possible. Irreversibility is often produced by missing clocks, missing authority, or asymmetric evidence demands.

It is the condition that irreversibility indices measure and that irreversible boundaries are drawn to prevent.
entries.scope: J. Decision states & edges. Where and how decisions flip from reversible to permanent.
operationalTests: A state is classified as irreversible when reversal is practically unavailable, not only theoretically impossible.
The mechanism producing irreversibility (missing clock, authority, or evidence) is named.
entries.genealogy: Distinguishes practical irreversibility from theoretical possibility.

entries.title: Backstop
entries.bodyHtml:
A guaranteed fallback mechanism that triggers when the main process fails—timeouts, automatic approvals, emergency restoration, or external review. Backstops prevent the silent failure of the primary path.

They are the implementation of safe pause and the guarantee behind time-to-halt.
entries.scope: J. Decision states & edges. Where and how decisions flip from reversible to permanent.
operationalTests: Every critical path has a fallback that triggers automatically on failure.
A backstop is tested end-to-end, not specified in a runbook.
entries.genealogy: Makes graceful failure a designed guarantee rather than an aspiration.

entries.title: Rollback
entries.bodyHtml:
A designed ability to revert the system to a prior safe state—restoring access, undoing propagation, correcting records—ideally with minimal friction. Rollback is the technical face of reversibility.

It is bounded by time-to-restore and depends on restoration completeness.
entries.scope: J. Decision states & edges. Where and how decisions flip from reversible to permanent.
operationalTests: A prior safe state is reachable without disproportionate friction.
Rollback covers downstream propagation, not only the original record.
entries.genealogy: Turns reversal from a hope into an engineered operation.

entries.title: Auto-close / Auto-renew / Auto-share
entries.bodyHtml:
Default state transitions that happen without active consent—closing claims, renewing contracts, expanding data use—often presented as convenience while functioning as governance by inertia. They are defaults as governance in action.

Each silent transition is a site where meaningful control is quietly surrendered.
entries.scope: J. Decision states & edges. Where and how decisions flip from reversible to permanent.
operationalTests: No consequential state transition happens without active, recent consent.
An auto-transition is audited for who benefited and who lost control.
entries.genealogy: Names the inertia defaults that convert convenience into coercion.

categories.heading: K. System patterns & anti-patterns
categories.descriptionHtml: Recurring structures institutions build, most of them ways that process, tone, or disclosure stands in for remedy.

entries.title: Heroism-Dependent Systems
entries.bodyHtml:
Systems that rely on extraordinary effort, unpaid care, or silent sacrifice to function. They mask poor stoppability and high failure load.

The heroism is a fallback nobody wrote down, which is normalized dependence in its human form. Counting that effort into dependency state makes it a budget item rather than a virtue.
entries.scope: K. System patterns & anti-patterns. Recurring structures institutions build, most of them ways that process, tone, or disclosure stands in for remedy.

entries.title: Empathy Surrogacy
entries.bodyHtml: Simulated warmth—chatbots, scripted apologies, tone guidelines—used to mask structural harm or delay fixes. Empathy surrogacy diverts attention from repair and weakens contestability by substituting sentiment for remedy.
entries.scope: K. System patterns & anti-patterns. Recurring structures institutions build, most of them ways that process, tone, or disclosure stands in for remedy.

entries.title: Error Cascades
entries.bodyHtml:
Small automated mistakes that amplify across the system through retries, shared dependencies, or blind handoffs. Error cascades are rarely one bug: they are chain reactions in tightly coupled workflows.

Containment depends on ethical interrupts, clear rollback boundaries, and SLJs that trigger action before harms compound.
examples: A flawed fraud rule mislabels transactions, which triggers automatic account locks, support backlog spikes, and delayed rent payments.
entries.scope: K. System patterns & anti-patterns. Recurring structures institutions build, most of them ways that process, tone, or disclosure stands in for remedy.

entries.title: Invisible Fallbacks
entries.bodyHtml: Hidden behaviors that appear under stress—shadow queues, silent throttling, or undocumented overrides. Invisible fallbacks obscure ethical load paths and should be surfaced through graceful rollback lanes and rehearsed in maintenance windows.
entries.scope: K. System patterns & anti-patterns. Recurring structures institutions build, most of them ways that process, tone, or disclosure stands in for remedy.

entries.title: Dead-User Zones
entries.bodyHtml: Places where people affected by decisions cannot contest, appeal, or exit—opaque rankings, automated bans, or unmoderated queues. Closing dead-user zones requires widening the permission surface and raising appeal passage rates.
entries.scope: K. System patterns & anti-patterns. Recurring structures institutions build, most of them ways that process, tone, or disclosure stands in for remedy.

entries.title: Moral Lock-In
entries.bodyHtml:
When harmful defaults become entrenched through dependencies, network effects, or contracts that block reform. Moral lock-in is prevented by moral feature gating, contestability, and continuous moral drift control.

Lock-in usually begins as normalized dependence: reliance nobody records until reform requires reversing it. Tracking dependency state turns lock-in from a late discovery into a measurement taken early.
entries.scope: K. System patterns & anti-patterns. Recurring structures institutions build, most of them ways that process, tone, or disclosure stands in for remedy.

entries.title: Withdrawal Rehearsal
entries.bodyHtml:
A scheduled exercise in which a system is stood down, in whole or in a bounded slice, and the fallback carries real work for a stated period. The rehearsal produces timings, failures, and a list of what did not work.

It matters because untested withdrawal is a claim rather than a capacity. Rehearsal is the evidence that separates operational reversibility from a diagram, and it is how preserved capacity is kept alive rather than merely listed.
entries.scope: K. System patterns & anti-patterns. Recurring structures institutions build, most of them ways that process, tone, or disclosure stands in for remedy.
operationalTests: Rehearsals are scheduled on a cadence and are not cancelled for load.
The rehearsal uses production volume for a bounded slice, not a synthetic replay.
Findings become funded work items with owners, not observations in a report.
entries.genealogy: The practice that produces evidence for Laws VI and XII, adapted from disaster recovery exercises to the withdrawal of a depended-upon system.

minimumEvidence.artifact: A rehearsal plan and report with scope, duration, timings, and findings.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A rehearsal completed at production volume with the fallback carrying the work.
minimumEvidence.metric: Interval since last rehearsal, and share of findings closed before the next one.

entries.title: Polite Coercion
entries.bodyHtml:
Coercion delivered through soothing language and “helpful” workflows that make refusal costly or stigmatized. Polite coercion is power that avoids looking like power.

It pairs with tone policing and launders coercive consent through legitimacy laundering.
entries.scope: K. System patterns & anti-patterns. Recurring structures institutions build, most of them ways that process, tone, or disclosure stands in for remedy.
operationalTests: A workflow is scored by the real cost of refusal, not by its tone.
Soothing language that raises refusal cost is flagged as coercion.
entries.genealogy: Makes the soothing register of coercion visible as coercion.

entries.title: Documentation Loop / Resubmission Loop
entries.bodyHtml:
A repeating pattern where the system continually requests more evidence or re-uploads without moving toward a binding decision. Often used to shift labor onto claimants and to manufacture dropout.

It is burden transfer with a smile, and a feeder of attrition as resolution.
entries.scope: K. System patterns & anti-patterns. Recurring structures institutions build, most of them ways that process, tone, or disclosure stands in for remedy.
operationalTests: Repeated requests must move a claim closer to a binding decision.
A request that does not advance the decision is flagged as a loop, not progress.
entries.genealogy: Makes the resubmission loop legible as delay machinery.

entries.title: Precision Demands
entries.bodyHtml:
Requests for ever-greater specificity that function less as truth-seeking and more as denial hooks—ways to keep a case non-objectified or non-decidable. Precision demands are a technique of delay.

They prevent object formation and are the mirror of documentation loops.
entries.scope: K. System patterns & anti-patterns. Recurring structures institutions build, most of them ways that process, tone, or disclosure stands in for remedy.
operationalTests: A specificity request is scored by whether it advances or stalls the decision.
A demand that cannot be met is flagged as a denial hook, not due diligence.
entries.genealogy: Separates genuine evidentiary need from precision used as a stall.

entries.title: Procedural Alibi
entries.bodyHtml:
A record of “process” used to defend outcomes (“we followed procedure”) even when the procedure cannot bind the institution to remedy. The alibi is the trace of activity, not accountability.

It is the paper form of procedural force without power, and the close cousin of paper compliance.
entries.scope: K. System patterns & anti-patterns. Recurring structures institutions build, most of them ways that process, tone, or disclosure stands in for remedy.
operationalTests: Procedure is scored by whether it can bind the institution, not by whether it was followed.
A “we followed procedure” defense is tested against remedy, not against the process log.
entries.genealogy: Exposes procedure-as-alibi where activity substitutes for remedy.

entries.title: Tone Policing (as Governance Technology)
entries.bodyHtml:
The use of “appropriate tone” requirements to control access to remedy—penalizing anger, urgency, neurodivergent communication, or exhaustion. Tone policing converts distress into disqualification.

It is the affective edge of polite coercion, and it defeats affect invariance.
entries.scope: K. System patterns & anti-patterns. Recurring structures institutions build, most of them ways that process, tone, or disclosure stands in for remedy.
operationalTests: Access to remedy does not depend on the claimant’s tone or composure.
A distress signal is treated as information, not as a disqualifier.
entries.genealogy: Makes the affective gate on remedy visible as a governance mechanism.

entries.title: Dropout-as-legitimation
entries.bodyHtml:
When systems treat nonresponse, fatigue, or disappearance as consent or closure (“case closed—no reply”), laundering coercion into “resolved.” Dropout becomes the mechanism that protects the institution.

It is attrition as resolution wearing the face of user inaction, producing unearned closure.
entries.scope: K. System patterns & anti-patterns. Recurring structures institutions build, most of them ways that process, tone, or disclosure stands in for remedy.
operationalTests: Nonresponse is never treated as consent or as a decision.
Dropout is investigated as a possible coercion outcome, not logged as “resolved.”
entries.genealogy: Reads silence as an outcome the system manufactured, not as user choice.

entries.title: Churn (as Closure Mechanism)
entries.bodyHtml:
The engineered cycling of people through forms, queues, and handoffs until they give up, miss a deadline, or become “inactive,” allowing the system to close without settlement. Churn is manufactured attrition.

It is the machinery behind dropout-as-legitimation and a producer of attrition as resolution.
entries.scope: K. System patterns & anti-patterns. Recurring structures institutions build, most of them ways that process, tone, or disclosure stands in for remedy.
operationalTests: Handoff counts are audited as a closure mechanism, not as service.
A case that closes from inactivity is re-opened on the merits, not closed silently.
entries.genealogy: Names the deliberate cycling that converts process friction into closure.

entries.title: Paper Compliance / Checkbox Governance
entries.bodyHtml:
Compliance regimes focused on producing documentation of doing the right thing rather than mechanisms that can prevent harm or force remedy. The paperwork stands in for power.

It is the institutional form of procedural alibi, and the failure mode behind compliance collapse.
entries.scope: K. System patterns & anti-patterns. Recurring structures institutions build, most of them ways that process, tone, or disclosure stands in for remedy.
operationalTests: Compliance is scored by a mechanism’s effect on harm, not by its documentation.
A checklist without a binding effect is flagged as paper, not compliance.
entries.genealogy: Distinguishes documentary compliance from enforceable compliance.

entries.title: Transparency Theater
entries.bodyHtml:
Disclosures that do not increase contestability—more text, more dashboards, more “explanations”—without deadlines, authority, or reversal paths. Visibility substitutes for enforceability.

It is the disclosure form of paper compliance and the complement of explainability decoy.
entries.scope: K. System patterns & anti-patterns. Recurring structures institutions build, most of them ways that process, tone, or disclosure stands in for remedy.
operationalTests: A disclosure is scored by whether it increases contestability, not by its volume.
Visibility without a reversal path is flagged as theater, not transparency.
entries.genealogy: Exposes visibility as a substitute for the enforceability it should enable.

entries.title: Explainability Decoy
entries.bodyHtml:
A focus on explaining model decisions that distracts from the harder question: can the decision be contested, reversed, and time-bounded? The decoy offers epistemics where governance is needed.

It redirects attention from explainability for accountability toward explanation for its own sake.
entries.scope: K. System patterns & anti-patterns. Recurring structures institutions build, most of them ways that process, tone, or disclosure stands in for remedy.
operationalTests: An explanation is scored by whether it enables contestation and reversal.
Explainability effort is measured against its effect on remedy, not its detail.
entries.genealogy: Names the substitution of explanation for enforceable accountability.

entries.title: Human-in-the-loop (as Legitimacy Artifact)
entries.bodyHtml:
A human reviewer inserted to create legitimacy while lacking binding authority, deadlines, or meaningful discretion. The loop becomes a comfort signal, not a power shift.

It is the person-shaped form of rubber-stamp review, distinguished from real binding authority.
entries.scope: K. System patterns & anti-patterns. Recurring structures institutions build, most of them ways that process, tone, or disclosure stands in for remedy.
operationalTests: A human reviewer’s authority and deadlines are specified, not assumed.
A loop that cannot change state is flagged as a legitimacy artifact.
entries.genealogy: Makes the human-in-the-loop visible as a legitimacy device when it lacks power.
